LAPLEX: The FFT of Learnable Laplace Kernels

Łukasz Struski Email: lukasz.struski@uj.edu.pl Affiliation:  Faculty of Mathematics and Computer Science, Jagiellonian University, Kraków, Poland    Hanna Blazhko Email: hanna.blazhko@student.uj.edu.pl Affiliation:  Faculty of Mathematics and Computer Science, Jagiellonian University, Kraków, Poland    Piotr Kubaty Email: piotr.kubaty@doctoral.uj.edu.pl Affiliation:  Faculty of Mathematics and Computer Science, Jagiellonian University, Kraków, Poland Affiliation:  Doctoral School of Exact and Natural Sciences, Jagiellonian University, Kraków, Poland    Jacek Tabor Email: jacek.tabor@uj.edu.pl Affiliation:  Faculty of Mathematics and Computer Science, Jagiellonian University, Kraków, Poland Affiliation:  Centre for Credible Artificial Intelligence, Warsaw University of Technology, Poland
Abstract

Fast linear algebra in deep learning usually comes with a choice: fixed geometry and exact computation, as in the Fourier transform, or adaptive geometry paid for by dense parameters, random features, or low-rank surrogates. To move beyond this trade-off, we introduce LAPLEX, a class of exact, trainable (phased) Laplace-kernel operators.

A LAPLEX layer is a typically full-rank dense matrix, implicitly defined by learnable coordinate anchors, with FFT-like scaling. Consequently, it supports trainable matrix–vector operations at vector dimensions up to 10910^{9} on modern GPUs. As a neural layer, it yields compact projections and classification heads interpretable as soft, trainable routing models. The same primitive also serves as an efficient Gram operator, enabling high-dimensional covariance models on flattened images of dimension 3⋅1063\cdot 10^{6} that preserve visible spatial structure without imposing convolutional bias. These applications reflect a single principle: dense geometry can be learned without storing a dense matrix, which enables data-adaptive global interactions in regimes where ordinary dense layers are out of reach. In this sense, LAPLEX separates expressivity from storage cost: it behaves like a dense trainable matrix, but is represented and applied through a small structured set of parameters.

1 Introduction

Modern machine-learning systems increasingly operate in regimes where the ambient dimension reaches millions or billions, and the bottleneck is no longer only statistical efficiency but also the wall-clock cost of linear operations: applying matrices, computing Gram operators, and mixing features. These operations are often treated as routine infrastructure, yet they determine which models can be trained, which kernels can be used exactly, and which high-dimensional representations fit on hardware at all. Standard scaling techniques typically sacrifice at least one of the properties we want: exactness, learnability, and near-linear scaling. Low-rank methods (18, 31) retain dense, basis-dependent interactions at 𝒪⁡(n​k)\mathcal{O}(nk) memory; randomized sketches (1, 2, 23) act on a fixed indexing and trade exactness for scalability; sparse methods (9, 17) can break hardware regularity and are difficult to train end-to-end; classical fast transforms such as the FFT are exact and cheap, but fixed.

The hidden cost of basis-dependent operators.

A dense linear map A:ℝn→ℝkA\colon\mathbb{R}^{n}\!\to\!\mathbb{R}^{k} consists of kk inner products, so every input–output coordinate pair receives its own algebraic identity. Even a low-rank operator with k≪nk\ll n still stores n×kn\!\times\!k coefficients: the rank compresses the image, but not the input basis. This is why low-rank parameterizations such as LoRA (18) cannot escape an 𝒪⁡(n​k)\mathcal{O}(nk) memory footprint. A different route is to parameterize operators through the indices themselves. The FFT is the canonical example: exact, free of learnable per-coordinate weights, and 𝒪⁡(n​log⁡n)\mathcal{O}(n\log n). Sketches such as CountSketch (2), Random Fourier Features (23), and Johnson–Lindenstrauss projections (1) follow a related index-level philosophy, but they act on a fixed indexing and cannot adapt how coordinates are matched. They are efficient, but rigid.

Our idea: index-level operators that can learn their input geometry.

We pursue operators that retain the memory advantages of index-based computation but, unlike the FFT or CountSketch, can learn how to align, shift, and permute coordinates. Under a natural optimization formulation, the resulting object is a single structured matrix: the Laplace-kernel matrix

LAPLEX​(a,b)=[exp⁡(−|ai−bj|)]i,j,\mbox{LAPLEX}(a,b)\;=\;\bigl[\exp(-|a_{i}-b_{j}|)\bigr]_{i,j},

which, in a natural limiting regime, encodes all permutations of the coordinate set while using only 𝒪⁡(n)\mathcal{O}(n) parameters. Despite its apparent density, matrix–vector and Gram products with LAPLEX can be computed exactly, with no approximation, in 𝒪⁡(n)\mathcal{O}(n) time11 1 During training, sorting gives 𝒪⁡(n​log⁡n)\mathcal{O}(n\log n) time. and memory, without ever materializing the matrix. The algorithm is fully parallel: in our experiments, wall-clock time remains almost flat until the GPU saturates; see Fig. 1.

The resulting primitive is useful wherever a model needs a large linear map but cannot afford a dense one. In representation learning, LAPLEX can serve as a trainable projection from massive feature vectors to compact embeddings. In fine-tuning, it can replace dense or LoRA-style heads with structured class–feature alignments. In kernel methods, attention, and second-order optimization, its exact Gram operator makes computations available that would otherwise require Nyström, random-feature, or low-rank approximations. As a proof of concept, we train a Gaussian density model on flattened ××10243\!\times\!1024\!\times\!1024 images; see Fig. 4. The learned density preserves visible pixel correspondence despite operating on flattened images. The common pattern is that LAPLEX keeps the algebraic regularity of a fast transform while making the coordinate system itself learnable.

Contributions.

LAPLEX combines the efficiency and regularity of fast transforms with learnable geometry over coordinates. Unlike existing approaches, it does not rely on approximation, dimensionality reduction, or irregular sparsity, while retaining exactness and near-linear time and memory complexity. This shift from parameterizing matrices to parameterizing index interactions makes large-scale linear algebra both tractable and adaptive. Operations that were previously bottlenecks, such as exact kernel application or Gram computation, become practical building blocks in high-dimensional models.

  • •

    We identify the basis-dependence limitation of low-rank operators and motivate index-level, permutation-aware operators as a principled alternative.

  • •

    We show that the resulting Laplace-kernel matrix LAPLEX uses 𝒪⁡(n)\mathcal{O}(n) parameters while encoding all coordinate permutations in a natural limiting regime.

  • •

    We give an exact, fully parallel 𝒪⁡(n​log⁡n)\mathcal{O}(n\log n) algorithm22 2 We provide both a native PyTorch implementation and a CUDA-optimized implementation. for matrix–vector and Gram products with LAPLEX using 𝒪⁡(n)\mathcal{O}(n) memory, without materializing the matrix, enabling dimensions up to 10910^{9}.

  • •

    We show empirically that LAPLEX matches FFT-class scaling while functioning efficiently as a drop-in structured layer in modern machine-learning systems.

Paper organization.

We organize the paper around the roles that LAPLEX plays. Sec. 2 gives a compact map of the nearest literature. Sec. 3 develops the exact scan algebra for matrix–vector and Gram products. Sec. 4 shows why this algebra changes the feasible high-dimensional regime, through primitive GPU scaling and a density-modeling experiment based on exact Gramians. Sec. 5 studies LAPLEX as a learnable relaxation of index routing and tests this view through structured projections against CountSketch and related baselines. Sec. 6 explains how Toeplitz–FFT and RFF arise as fixed-grid and Monte Carlo views of the same Laplace kernel. Finally, Sec. 7 evaluates anchor geometry in neural classification heads, and Sec. 8 discusses limitations and open directions.

2 Related Work

We focus on the closest algorithmic alternatives: exact fast transforms, randomized kernel approximations, low-rank parameterizations, and sparsity. The useful comparison is not only asymptotic complexity, but also what each method fixes in advance: a grid, a random map, a feature count, a rank, or a sparsity pattern.

Exact fast transforms. The FFT (5, 11) and Toeplitz or circulant methods (14) achieve near-linear exact multiplication by exploiting fixed grid structure. For the Laplace kernel, the uniform-grid choice ai=bi=i​Δa_{i}=b_{i}=i\Delta makes LAPLEX​(a,b)\mbox{LAPLEX}(a,b) Toeplitz, so Toeplitz–FFT is a fast algorithm for this rigid slice of our family. This is the exact baseline for the fixed-grid case; learned anchors ask for a different primitive.

Sketches and random features. CountSketch and related sketches (2, 3, 6) compress coordinates through fixed or randomized routing, while Random Fourier Features (23) approximate shift-invariant kernels through Monte Carlo spectral features and underlie several linear attention methods (4, 19, 22). LAPLEX connects to both: CountSketch-like maps appear as zero-temperature limits (App. A), while RFF is a sampled surrogate of the same Laplace kernel that LAPLEX applies exactly.

Low-rank and sparse neural operators. Nyström methods (7, 13, 33) and low-rank adapters such as LoRA (18) reduce cost by introducing an explicit rank bottleneck. Sparse neural methods (9, 10, 17, 26) reduce parameter count, but practical speedups depend on sparsity pattern and hardware support. LAPLEX instead keeps a dense interaction implicit: parameters live in the anchors, and computation proceeds through regular sorted scans.

3 Exact Laplace algebra: matvecs and Gram operators

The representational picture would be much less interesting if every use of LAPLEX​(a,b)\mbox{LAPLEX}(a,b) required forming the dense matrix. The algorithmic fact that makes the construction useful is that one-dimensional Laplace interactions are dense but ordered. After sorting anchors, each side of an anchor sees an exponentially rescaled prefix or suffix sum. This turns a dense kernel operator into a scan computation. The consequence is the central computational promise of LAPLEX: we can work with dense, trainable kernel interactions at dimensions where the matrix itself is not an object one can store. Matrix–vector products become near-linear; weighted Gram matrices keep only the unavoidable quadratic output cost.

Overview of the approach.

We first show the symmetric case a=ba=b, where sorted anchors reduce the operator exactly to prefix and suffix scans. We then handle the rectangular case a≠ba\neq b by bucketing the bb-anchors into intervals induced by sorted aa and aggregating their contributions before applying the same scan primitive. The weighted Gram decomposition follows the same logic: the intermediate anchors are summarized once, and the full Gram matrix is assembled from ordered cumulative statistics. All reductions are differentiable except for the usual piecewise-constant sorting order, as in sorting-based neural operators.

Symmetric case: a prefix-scan primitive.

For a=ba=b, the kernel matrix is

A=LAPLEX​(a)=[exp⁡(−|ai−aj|)]i​j.A=\mbox{LAPLEX}(a)=[\exp(-|a_{i}-a_{j}|)]_{ij}.

Assume a1≤a2≤⋯≤ana_{1}\leq a_{2}\leq\cdots\leq a_{n}. Then

Ai​j={exp⁡(aj−ai),i≥j,exp⁡(ai−aj),i<j.A_{ij}=\begin{cases}\exp(a_{j}-a_{i}),&i\geq j,\\[4.0pt] \exp(a_{i}-a_{j}),&i<j.\end{cases}

Decompose the matrix into lower and upper triangular parts: A​x=tril⁡(A)​x+triu⁡(A,1)​xAx=\mathrm{tril}(A)x+\mathrm{triu}(A,1)x. For the lower triangular part,

yi=∑j≤iexp⁡(aj−ai)​xj.y_{i}=\sum_{j\leq i}\exp(a_{j}-a_{i})\,x_{j}.

This satisfies the recurrence

yi+1=∑j≤i+1exp⁡(aj−ai+1)​xj=xi+1+exp⁡(ai−ai+1)​∑j≤iexp⁡(aj−ai)​xj,y_{i+1}=\sum_{j\leq i+1}\exp(a_{j}-a_{i+1})\,x_{j}=x_{i+1}+\exp(a_{i}-a_{i+1})\sum_{j\leq i}\exp(a_{j}-a_{i})\,x_{j},

or yi+1=xi+1+exp⁡(ai−ai+1)​yiy_{i+1}=x_{i+1}+\exp(a_{i}-a_{i+1})y_{i}. A prefix scan evaluates this recurrence in 𝒪⁡(n)\mathcal{O}(n) work and 𝒪⁡(log⁡n)\mathcal{O}(\log n) parallel depth; a reverse scan handles the upper triangular part. Thus sorted symmetric multiplication is linear in time and memory, and sorting raises the total cost to 𝒪⁡(n​log⁡n)\mathcal{O}(n\log n).

General case: exact aggregation over intervals.

The asymmetric case is where LAPLEX departs from classical Toeplitz algebra. The anchors bb need not lie on the grid of aa; they can be irregular, batched, or learned. Each bjb_{j} falls into one interval between neighbouring sorted aa-anchors. Inside that interval, its contribution to all points on the left and all points on the right has a separable exponential form (see Fig.2). We therefore aggregate the local contributions into two vectors and propagate them through the symmetric scan primitive. Proofs of the matrix–vector reductions are in App. B; the Gram proof is in App. C.

Theorem 1.

Assume a1≤⋯≤ana_{1}\leq\cdots\leq a_{n} and extend with a0=−∞a_{0}=-\infty, an+1=+∞a_{n+1}=+\infty. For i=1,…,n+1i=1,\ldots,n+1 define the intervals

Pi=[ai−1,ai).P_{i}=[a_{i-1},a_{i}).

Given b,x∈ℝkb,x\in\mathbb{R}^{k}, define vectors u,v∈ℝnu,v\in\mathbb{R}^{n} by

ui=∑j:bj∈Pixjeai−bj,vi=∑j:bj∈Pixjebj−ai.u_{i}=\sum_{j:b_{j}\in P_{i}}x_{j}\,e^{\,a_{i}-b_{j}},\qquad v_{i}=\sum_{j:b_{j}\in P_{i}}x_{j}\,e^{\,b_{j}-a_{i}}.

Then

LAPLEX​(a,b)​x=triu⁡(K)​u+tril⁡(K)​v,\mbox{LAPLEX}(a,b)x=\mathrm{triu}(K)\,u+\mathrm{tril}(K)\,v,

where K=LAPLEX​(a)K=\mbox{LAPLEX}(a).

Complexity.

If sorted anchors are already available, interval assignment and local aggregation cost 𝒪⁡(k)\mathcal{O}(k), and the two triangular scan products cost 𝒪⁡(n)\mathcal{O}(n). Sorting gives 𝒪⁡(n​log⁡n+k​log⁡n)\mathcal{O}(n\log n+k\log n) time, and the storage remains linear in the number of anchors. In training, the sorted order can be reused across batches and the dual reduction in App. B dispatches through the shorter axis when nn and kk are imbalanced.

Computation of Gram matrix.

The same order structure also gives exact weighted Gram matrices. This is important because many downstream algorithms do not only apply a kernel operator; they need expressions of the form

M=A​diag⁡(D)​A⊤,A=LAPLEX​(a,b),D∈ℝ+k.M=A\operatorname{diag}(D)A^{\top},\quad A=\mbox{LAPLEX}(a,b),\quad D\in\mathbb{R}^{k}_{+}.

Such matrices appear in attention, kernel methods, Woodbury-accelerated Gaussian likelihoods, and Fisher or Gauss–Newton curvature approximations (19, 21, 23, 24, 32, 33). A naive computation pays 𝒪⁡(n2​k)\mathcal{O}(n^{2}k). For the Laplace kernel, the middle anchor set can again be summarized by interval-wise statistics, after which every entry of MM is recovered exactly from scan products and prefix sums.

We work in the same assumptions as in the previous theorem.

Theorem 2 (Exact Gram decomposition).

We define u,v,w∈ℝnu,v,w\in\mathbb{R}^{n} by

ui=∑bt∈Pie2​(bt−ai)​Dt,vi=∑bt∈Pie2​(ai−bt)​Dt,wi=∑bt∈PiDt.u_{i}=\sum_{b_{t}\in P_{i}}e^{2(b_{t}-a_{i})}D_{t},\quad v_{i}=\sum_{b_{t}\in P_{i}}e^{2(a_{i}-b_{t})}D_{t},\quad w_{i}=\sum_{b_{t}\in P_{i}}D_{t}.

Put U=tril⁡(K)​uU=\mathrm{tril}(K)u, V=triu⁡(K)​vV=\mathrm{triu}(K)v for K=LAPLEX​(2​a)K=\mbox{LAPLEX}(2a). We also define WW by Wi=∑j≤iwjW_{i}=\sum_{j\leq i}w_{j}.

Then for i≥ji\geq j, the entries of M=A​diag⁡(D)​A⊤M=A\operatorname{diag}(D)A^{\top} are given by

Mi​j=exp⁡(aj−ai)​(Uj+(Wi−Wj)+Vi),M_{ij}=\exp(a_{j}-a_{i})\Bigl(U_{j}+(W_{i}-W_{j})+V_{i}\Bigr),

with symmetric extension Mj​i=Mi​jM_{ji}=M_{ij}.

Proof in App. C. The cost is 𝒪⁡(n2+k​log⁡k)\mathcal{O}(n^{2}+k\log k): the n2n^{2} term is the output size of the full Gram matrix, while the dependence on the intermediate anchor set remains near-linear.

Phased Laplace kernels.

For neural layers it is often advantageous adding the phase without losing the fast algebra. Given phase anchors ϕ∈ℝn,ψ∈ℝk\phi\in\mathbb{R}^{n},\psi\in\mathbb{R}^{k} we define

OPENLAPLEX​(a,ϕ,b,ψ)j​k=exp⁡(−|aj−bk|))⋅cos⁡(ϕj−ψk),\mbox{LAPLEX}(a,\phi;b,\psi)_{jk}\;=\;\exp\!\bigl(-|a_{j}-b_{k}|)\bigr)\cdot\cos(\phi_{j}-\psi_{k}),

so the standard kernel is the special case α=β=0\alpha=\beta=0. Angle-sum identities reduce each phased matrix–vector or weighted Gram operation to a constant number of non-phased LAPLEX calls plus 𝒪⁡(n+k)\mathcal{O}(n+k) pointwise phase modulation. The phases are ordinary trainable parameters, and their gradients flow through the same exact scan computation.

4 Scaling consequences: GPU primitives and high-dimensional Gramians

The algebra above is meant to change the feasible regime, not merely the notation. We therefore separate the consequences from the derivation. The first test asks whether the scan primitive behaves like a fast transform on hardware; the second asks whether exact weighted Gramians can support a meaningful Gaussian model in hundreds of thousands of dimensions.

4.1 Primitive scaling on GPU

The systems question is whether the scan algebra behaves like a fast transform on real hardware. We measure matrix–vector multiplication X​K​(a,b)XK(a,b). The dense baseline explicitly materializes the n×nn\times n kernel matrix and calls torch.matmul. All experiments run on a single NVIDIA H100 in float32; full timing details, memory accounting, and OOM rules are given in App. D.

Scaling and memory.

Figure 3 is the basic scalability test. The dense baseline stops being a method once the n×nn\times n kernel no longer fits in memory; LAPLEX continues as an implicit operator and scales smoothly to n=220n=2^{20}. At the largest size where both methods fit, LAPLEX is already ∼65×\sim\!65\times faster on the forward pass, ∼430×\sim\!430\times faster on forward+backward, and uses ∼100×\sim\!100\times less peak memory. This is the practical difference between storing a dense interaction and computing it as a fast transform.

Numerical results.

The scan is not merely faster than dense float32; it is also more accurate against a dense float64 reference. Dense matmul sums nn terms in ordinary floating point, so its error grows like 𝒪⁡(n​ε)\mathcal{O}(n\varepsilon). The LAPLEX scan keeps exponential scale factors separate from mantissas and introduces only 𝒪⁡(ε)\mathcal{O}(\varepsilon) rounding per element (App. D.2). The same pattern holds beyond the square forward pass. The weighted Gram operator yields an asymptotic Θ⁡(n2/log⁡n)\Theta(n^{2}/\log n) speed-up over dense construction (App. D.5); asymmetric problems dispatch to the shorter axis (App. D.4); and even the pure-PyTorch CPU reference remains far faster than dense (App. D.6).

4.2 High-dimensional density modeling on DIV2K at dim≈𝟑⋅𝟏𝟎𝟔\boldsymbol{\approx 3\cdot 10^{6}}

To stress-test the Gram primitive at an extremely high data dimension, we fit Gaussian density models to flattened DIV2K-10241024 images (800800 training, 100100 validation), where each example is a 3,145,7283{,}145{,}728-dimensional vector (××31024\!\times\!1024\!\times\!3), again with no patches, convolutions, or positional encoding. At this scale even writing down an empirical covariance is hopeless (it would require ∼1013\sim\!10^{13} parameters); the question is whether a structured exact Gram operator still carries meaningful geometry once the data dimension reaches the multi-million regime.

Setup.

We use a low-rank-plus-diagonal Gaussian template

x=m+F​z+d⊙ε,x\;=\;m\;+\;F\,z\;+\;d\odot\varepsilon,

with z∼𝒩⁡(0,Ik)z\sim\mathcal{N}(0,I_{k}) and ε∼𝒩⁡(0,In)\varepsilon\sim\mathcal{N}(0,I_{n}). At a matched parameter budget we compare two parameterizations of FF: (i) a phased LAPLEX factor F=diag⁡(w)​A​LF=\mathrm{diag}(w)AL with AA a width-10001000 Laplace kernel and LL a lower-triangular Cholesky factor (13.613.6M trainable parameters); (ii) a freely trained dense low-rank factor F∈ℝn×klow−rankF\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times k_{\mathrm{low-rank}}} (15.715.7M trainable parameters at klow−rank=4k_{\mathrm{low-rank}}=4). Under this budget the dense baseline can only afford rank ∼4\sim\!4, whereas LAPLEX learns a rank-10001000 structured factor. Both models are trained for 2020 epochs with Adam and identical optimizer settings.

Takeaway.

Figure 4 gives the most visual demonstration of what the anchors learn. A LAPLEX covariance factor trained only on flat vectors discovers coherent spatial color structure: samples have contiguous regions, and the MAP reconstruction preserves the palm, beach and clouds silhouettes. The matched-budget dense low-rank baseline collapses to nearly uniform noise because its rank budget is too small to represent these correlations. The only place the spatial organization can live in the LAPLEX model is the learned anchor geometry, which is precisely the mechanism we want.

5 Learnable routing: CountSketch limits and structured projections

We first look at what the anchors represent. In LAPLEX, a matrix entry is large when two learned coordinates are close and small when they are far apart. At finite temperature this is a smooth matching rule; as the temperature goes to zero it becomes discrete equality routing. Thus the same object that behaves like a dense kernel in the forward pass also contains permutations, hashes, and sparse routing maps on its boundary.

For the temperature-scaled kernel

LAPLEXt(a,b)=[exp(−|ai−bj|/t)]i​j,\mbox{LAPLEX}_{t}(a,b)=[\exp(-|a_{i}-b_{j}|/t)]_{ij},

the limit t→0t\to 0 becomes an equality-routing matrix. Suitable anchor multiplicities recover permutations and CountSketch-like maps, while diagonal scalings and sparse replication recover arbitrary rectangular dense matrices (App. A). The important difference is that LAPLEX does not ask us to choose the routing map before training: the geometry is a continuous parameter of the model.

After the fast algebra is in place, the next question is what the anchors can represent. If anchor geometry is a learnable version of sketching, then it should preserve useful signal better than fixed sketches when inserted as a projection from a very high-dimensional input. We test this on flattened ImageNet10, where the input dimension is already 150,528150{,}528.

Structured input projections versus CountSketch

The test is intentionally unforgiving: each ImageNet10 image is flattened to d=××3=150,528d=224\!\times\!224\!\times\!3=150,528 coordinates, and the classifier sees only a projected vector of dimension m∈{25,100,500,1000}m\in\{25,100,500,1000\}. In a frozen regime, the projection is fixed and only the logistic head is trained, so the projection is judged by how much signal it preserves. In a trainable regime, LAPLEX anchors are optimized end-to-end and compared with an unconstrained dense projection at the same output dimension. Frozen competitors are CountSketch (2), PCA, and Gaussian random projections; the full τ\tau-sweep is in App. G.

Results.

Table 1 shows the expected hierarchy: PCA is strongest at small mm because it is fitted to the training set, while fixed random maps lose signal quickly. Among data-agnostic maps–CountSketch, Gaussian random projections, and frozen LAPLEX–LAPLEX is the most stable and becomes best at the largest mm. Even before learning the anchors, the smooth geometry is a richer alternative to a fixed hash.

The trainable columns are the more revealing part. Once anchors are learned for the task, LAPLEX matches or beats the dense projection at every mm while using Θ⁡(m+d)\Theta(m+d) rather than Θ⁡(m​d)\Theta(md) parameters. The gains are small but consistent across seeds. This is exactly the intended behavior: the operator does not merely compress the input; it learns a task-adapted coordinate matching in a space where a dense projection is expensive.

6 Restricted views: fixed grids and sampled features

The comparison with Toeplitz–FFT and Random Fourier Features is useful because these methods are not distant competitors. They are what the same Laplace interaction becomes after two different restrictions. If the anchors are frozen to a uniform grid, the matrix is Toeplitz and FFT gives an exact specialized solver. If the anchors are irregular but the kernel is replaced by a finite spectral expansion, we obtain RFF. LAPLEX sits between these views: the anchors can move, the kernel values remain exact, and the gradients with respect to the anchors are still available.

Toeplitz–FFT: the fixed-grid slice

On the uniform grid ai=bi=i​Δa_{i}=b_{i}=i\Delta, the Laplace matrix [exp⁡(−|ai−bj|)]i​j[\exp(-|a_{i}-b_{j}|)]_{ij} is Toeplitz. Toeplitz–FFT is therefore the right algorithm for this slice of the family. The point of the comparison is not to claim that a general learned-anchor primitive should beat a solver hand-built for a fixed grid. The point is sharper: when we leave the grid, do we only pay a constant factor, or do we lose the fast-transform regime?

Figure 5 shows the answer. LAPLEX, Toeplitz–FFT, and a raw cuFFT call lie on parallel 𝒪⁡(n​log⁡n)\mathcal{O}(n\log n) curves. The extra constant is the price of sorting and scanning arbitrary anchors; what it buys is a different object: not convolution on a prescribed grid, but a dense kernel operator whose coordinate system can be learned. The numerical picture is also favorable. On the very Toeplitz problem where the FFT baseline is exactly applicable, Fig. 14(b) (App. E.1) shows that LAPLEX has lower float32 error than both dense matmul and Toeplitz–FFT. Thus the learned-anchor extension does not trade away stability for flexibility.

The categorical difference is differentiability with respect to the grid. Toeplitz–FFT differentiates through the input vector, but the anchor locations are the fixed discretization that makes the matrix Toeplitz. LAPLEX differentiates through xx, aa, and bb. For models that learn coordinate systems, kernel nodes, attention anchors, or covariance factors, this is the difference between tuning values on a grid and learning the grid itself. CPU results, the differentiability table, and comparisons to NUFFT and FMM are in App. E.

RFF: the sampled surrogate

RFF (23) removes the grid restriction, but pays by turning the exact kernel into a Monte Carlo feature map. For k⁡(u−v)=exp⁡(−|u−v|)k(u-v)=\exp(-|u-v|), Bochner’s theorem gives k^D​(u,v)=2D​∑d=1Dcos⁡(wd​u+cd)​cos⁡(wd​v+cd)\widehat{k}_{D}(u,v)=\tfrac{2}{D}\sum_{d=1}^{D}\cos(w_{d}u+c_{d})\cos(w_{d}v+c_{d}) with Cauchy frequencies p⁡(w)=[π⁡(1+w2)]−1p(w)=[\pi(1+w^{2})]^{-1}. This is an approximation to the same Laplace kernel that LAPLEX applies exactly. The feature count DD therefore plays the role of an accuracy knob, while LAPLEX has no sampled feature dimension.

We test the favorable case for RFF: irregular anchors a,b∼𝒩⁡(0,1)a,b\sim\mathcal{N}(0,1), n=216n=2^{16}, B=1B=1, and a shift-invariant kernel with a known spectral density. Figure 6 shows why this approximation is not a substitute for an exact learned kernel primitive. RFF matches the runtime of LAPLEX only at very small DD, where the value error is still about 72%72\%. Reducing the error below 10%10\% requires D≥1024D\geq 1024, making RFF about 75×75\times slower.

The gradient story is even more decisive. Differentiating the RFF estimator with respect to anchors multiplies each term by the sampled Cauchy frequency wdw_{d}, whose second moment is infinite. The resulting anchor gradient estimator has unbounded variance; empirically, the bb-anchor gradient error does not reliably decrease with DD (App. F.2). For fixed features this may be acceptable. For learnable kernels it is the central failure mode: RFF gives a sampled view of the Laplace kernel, while LAPLEX keeps exact values and exact anchor gradients at the same 𝒪⁡(n​log⁡n)\mathcal{O}(n\log n) cost.

7 Learned anchor geometry in neural heads

The projection experiment tests LAPLEX as a high-dimensional compression map, and the density experiment tests it as a Gram/covariance primitive. We also want a familiar neural-network interface where the operator must replace a standard dense matrix.

A classification head provides a clean testbed for whether anchor geometry can replace dense class–feature interactions. We freeze the pretrained backbone and train only the final head. For Swin-T (20), the original head is a single linear map W∈ℝc×fW\in\mathbb{R}^{c\times f} with f=768f=768 and c=1000c=1000; for MaxViT-T (30), it is the linear component of a two-layer MLP.

As a full-parameter baseline, we train a randomly initialized dense head. The LAPLEX head is parameterized as a weighted sum of rr Laplace-kernel operators,

LAPLEX(r)=∑i=1rwi​Li,Li∈ℝc×f,\mathrm{LAPLEX}^{(r)}\;=\;\sum_{i=1}^{r}w_{i}\,L_{i},\qquad L_{i}\in\mathbb{R}^{c\times f},

where each LiL_{i} is a LAPLEX matrix parameterized by an independent anchor pair (ai,bi)(a_{i},b_{i}) and wiw_{i} are scalar mixing weights. As a low-parameter baseline, we compare against a low-rank factorization

LowRank(r)=U​V⊤,U∈ℝc×r,V∈ℝf×r.\mathrm{LowRank}^{(r)}=UV^{\!\top},\qquad U\in\mathbb{R}^{c\times r},\quad V\in\mathbb{R}^{f\times r}.

All heads are trained under the same optimization setup; full details are provided in App. H.

Results.

Table 2 shows a consistent separation between LAPLEX(r) and LowRank(r) across both backbones. At matched parameter budgets, LAPLEX(r) consistently achieves higher accuracy, with the largest gains at low rank. While LowRank(r) constrains representations through a shared low-dimensional bottleneck, LAPLEX(r) models class–feature interactions through a learned geometric kernel structure. Using only 1​–​5%1\text{--}5\% of the original head parameters, LAPLEX(16) approaches full-rank performance within a few points. Full curves and training details are reported in App. H.

8 Conclusions and Limitations

The main message of this paper is that fast transforms do not have to live on fixed coordinate systems. By parameterizing a dense operator through learnable Laplace anchors, LAPLEX keeps exact matrix–vector and Gram computations in near-linear time and linear memory while exposing the geometry itself to gradient-based learning. Uniform-grid Toeplitz–FFT is a rigid slice of this family; RFF is a Monte Carlo surrogate for the same kernel; CountSketch-like routing appear as limiting cases. LAPLEX connects these views with a single exact, differentiable operator.

The empirical results show why this matters. LAPLEX reaches scales where dense kernels cannot be materialized, follows FFT-class scaling beyond the uniform grid, improves float32 accuracy over standard dense and Toeplitz routes in the tested regime, and avoids the value/gradient trade-offs of random features. As a learnable layer it gives compact projections and classification heads; as a Gram primitive it enables high-dimensional covariance models that preserve visible spatial structure without convolutional bias. These are all instances of the same principle: dense geometry can be learned without storing a dense matrix.

Limitations. The current construction is still deliberately narrow. It uses one-dimensional Laplace anchors and sorting-based algorithms. Extending the same exactness to higher-dimensional anchor geometries, richer kernels, and more general learned metrics is the main mathematical direction. A second limitation is systems maturity: the implementation demonstrates the algorithmic regime, but large-scale attention blocks, optimizers, and generative models will require specialized kernels and careful architecture design. The broader opportunity is clear: make the geometry of fast linear algebra learnable.
