Appendix

Guide to the Appendix.

The appendix extends the main paper by providing theoretical, algorithmic, and empirical details underlying LAPLEX. Section A establishes expressivity, showing that LAPLEX recovers discrete routing (e.g., CountSketch) in limiting regimes and is universal for dense linear maps. Sections B and C present proofs of the fast scan-based algorithms for exact matrix–vector and weighted Gram computations, achieving near-linear complexity. Sections D and E give a full empirical and systems-level evaluation, including GPU/CPU benchmarks and comparisons to FFT-based methods, highlighting both efficiency and differentiability advantages. Section F analyzes Random Fourier Features, demonstrating their limitations in value accuracy and especially gradient estimation compared to LAPLEX. Finally, Sections G–I provide extended experimental results, covering projection tasks (Section G), structured classification heads (Section H), and high-dimensional density modeling (Section I), illustrating the practical benefits of learnable Laplace-kernel operators.

Appendix A Expressivity: CountSketch and dense matrices as limits of LAPLEX

The main text treats LAPLEX as a smooth, learnable fast transform. This section identifies what lies on the boundary of that smooth family. For the temperature-scaled Laplace kernel

LAPLEXt​(a,b)∈ℝm×n,[LAPLEXt​(a,b)]i​j=exp⁡(−|ai−bj|t),t>0,\mbox{LAPLEX}_{t}(a,b)\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times n},\qquad\bigl[\mbox{LAPLEX}_{t}(a,b)\bigr]_{ij}\;=\;\exp\!\left(-\frac{|a_{i}-b_{j}|}{t}\right),\qquad t>0,

with a∈ℝma\in\mathbb{R}^{m} and b∈ℝnb\in\mathbb{R}^{n}, the limit t→0t\to 0 is an equality-routing matrix. This immediately recovers permutations and CountSketch-style hashing when anchors are chosen as discrete labels (Prop. 1). With diagonal scalings and sparse replication, the same family is universal for arbitrary rectangular dense matrices (Thm. 3). Thus, LAPLEX should not be viewed as a narrowly specialized matrix class, but rather as a continuous family interpolating between sparse routing structures and dense linear operators, while admitting fast exact computation throughout the smooth Laplace regime.

A.1 Zero-temperature limit

In the low-temperature limit, the kernel matrix converges to a binary incidence matrix encoding the equality structure between the entries of aa and bb, as stated in the following lemma.

Lemma 1 (Zero-temperature limit).

Let a∈ℝma\in\mathbb{R}^{m} and b∈ℝnb\in\mathbb{R}^{n}. Then, for every i∈{1,…,m}i\in\{1,\dots,m\} and j∈{1,…,n}j\in\{1,\dots,n\},

limt→0[LAPLEXt(a,b)]i​j=𝟏{ai=bj}.\lim_{t\to 0}\bigl[\mbox{LAPLEX}_{t}(a,b)\bigr]_{ij}=\mathbf{1}\{a_{i}=b_{j}\}.

Equivalently, LAPLEXt​(a,b)\mbox{LAPLEX}_{t}(a,b) converges entrywise to the matching matrix M⁡(a,b)M(a,b) defined by

M(a,b)i​j=𝟏{ai=bj}.M(a,b)_{ij}=\mathbf{1}\{a_{i}=b_{j}\}.
Proof.

If ai=bja_{i}=b_{j} then exp(−|ai−bj|/t)=1\exp(-|a_{i}-b_{j}|/t)=1 for every t>0t>0. If ai≠bja_{i}\neq b_{j} then |ai−bj|=c>0|a_{i}-b_{j}|=c>0 and exp(−c/t)→0\exp(-c/t)\to 0 as t→0t\to 0. ∎

A.2 CountSketch as a special case

In the low-temperature limit, the kernel recovers a hashing-based aggregation scheme, as formalized in the following proposition.

Proposition 1 (CountSketch realization).

Let nn denote the input dimension and mm the sketch dimension, typically with m≪nm\ll n. Let h:{1,…,n}→{1,…,m}h:\{1,\dots,n\}\to\{1,\dots,m\} be a hash function and let s∈{±1}ns\in\{\pm 1\}^{n} be a sign vector. Choose pairwise distinct scalars c1,…,cmc_{1},\dots,c_{m} and define

ai=ci,bj=ch⁡(j).a_{i}=c_{i},\qquad b_{j}=c_{h(j)}.

Then for every x∈ℝnx\in\mathbb{R}^{n},

limt→0LAPLEXt(a,b)(s⊙x)=y,yi=∑j:h⁡(j)=isjxj.\lim_{t\to 0}\mbox{LAPLEX}_{t}(a,b)\,(s\odot x)\;=\;y,\qquad y_{i}\;=\;\sum_{j:\,h(j)=i}s_{j}\,x_{j}.

That is, CountSketch arises as the zero-temperature limit of the kernel architecture (with sign multiplication folded into the input).

Proof.

By Lemma 1 and the fact that {cr}\{c_{r}\} are distinct, limt→0[LAPLEXt(a,b)]i​j=𝟏{i=h(j)}\lim_{t\to 0}[\mbox{LAPLEX}_{t}(a,b)]_{ij}=\mathbf{1}\{i=h(j)\}. For the ii-th output coordinate, ∑j𝟏{i=h(j)}sjxj=∑j:h⁡(j)=isjxj\sum_{j}\mathbf{1}\{i=h(j)\}s_{j}x_{j}=\sum_{j:\,h(j)=i}s_{j}x_{j}, which is precisely CountSketch. ∎

A.3 Universality for rectangular matrices

Theorem 3 (Rectangular universality).

Let W∈ℝm×nW\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times n} be arbitrary. There exist a replication operator Rm:ℝn→ℝm​nR_{m}:\mathbb{R}^{n}\!\to\!\mathbb{R}^{mn}, a diagonal matrix DW∈ℝm​n×m​nD_{W}\in\mathbb{R}^{mn\times mn}, and vectors a∈ℝma\in\mathbb{R}^{m}, b∈ℝm​nb\in\mathbb{R}^{mn} such that

W=(limt→0LAPLEXt​(a,b))​DW​Rm.W\;=\;\Bigl(\lim_{t\to 0}\mbox{LAPLEX}_{t}(a,b)\Bigr)\,D_{W}\,R_{m}.

The kernel architecture is therefore universal for all linear maps ℝn→ℝm\mathbb{R}^{n}\!\to\!\mathbb{R}^{m}.

Proof.

Choose pairwise distinct scalars c1,…,cmc_{1},\dots,c_{m} and set ai=cia_{i}=c_{i}. Index replicas by pairs (i,j)(i,j) with i∈{1,…,m}i\in\{1,\dots,m\} and j∈{1,…,n}j\in\{1,\dots,n\}, and define

(Rm​x)(i,j)=xj,(DW)(i,j),(i,j)=Wi​j,b(i,j)=ci.(R_{m}x)_{(i,j)}=x_{j},\qquad(D_{W})_{(i,j),(i,j)}=W_{ij},\qquad b_{(i,j)}=c_{i}.

By Lemma 1,

limt→0[LAPLEXt(a,b)]r,(i,j)=𝟏{cr=ci}=𝟏{r=i}.\lim_{t\to 0}[\mbox{LAPLEX}_{t}(a,b)]_{r,(i,j)}=\mathbf{1}\{c_{r}=c_{i}\}=\mathbf{1}\{r=i\}.

Thus the kernel groups all replicas with the same first index ii, and the rr-th output coordinate becomes

∑i,j𝟏{r=i}Wi​jxj=∑jWr​jxj=(Wx)r.\sum_{i,j}\mathbf{1}\{r=i\}\,W_{ij}\,x_{j}=\sum_{j}W_{rj}\,x_{j}=(Wx)_{r}.

∎

The proof shows that no output aggregation operator is needed: the kernel itself sums all replicas with the same target index.

A.4 Interpretation

The two results above sketch a continuous bridge between smooth structured kernels at positive temperature and discrete combinatorial routing in the limit t→0t\to 0. At low temperature, LAPLEXt​(a,b)\mbox{LAPLEX}_{t}(a,b) acts as a sparse hash table determined by equality patterns – recovering CountSketch and arbitrary discrete routings as special cases. Adding replication and diagonal scaling makes the family universal for arbitrary rectangular matrices. Computationally, all the building blocks remain cheap: diagonal maps and replications cost 𝒪⁡(n)\mathcal{O}(n), and LAPLEXt​(a,b)\mbox{LAPLEX}_{t}(a,b) admits the fast multiplication algorithm of App. B. A composition of a few such layers is therefore both highly expressive and asymptotically efficient.

Appendix B Fast matrix–vector multiplication: proofs and complexity

This section proves the two reduction theorems announced in Sec. 3 and gives the exact complexity in both regimes. Everything rests on one primitive: an exponentially weighted prefix/suffix scan over a sorted vector. We describe it first in Sec. B.1, then handle the two dispatch branches: Sec. B.2 reduces the general ℝn→ℝk\mathbb{R}^{n}\!\to\!\mathbb{R}^{k} matvec to that primitive when n≤kn\leq k (sort and scan along the shorter aa-axis), and Sec. B.3 treats the dual case n≥kn\geq k (sort and scan along the shorter bb-axis). The combined complexity is summarized in Sec. B.4.

B.1 Symmetric case: prefix-scan reduction

Let a∈ℝna\in\mathbb{R}^{n} with a1≤⋯≤ana_{1}\leq\cdots\leq a_{n} and write

A=LAPLEX​(a)=[exp⁡(−|ai−aj|)]i​j.A\;=\;\mbox{LAPLEX}(a)\;=\;\bigl[\exp(-|a_{i}-a_{j}|)\bigr]_{ij}.

For i≥ji\geq j, Ai​j=exp⁡(aj−ai)A_{ij}=\exp(a_{j}-a_{i}); for i<ji<j, Ai​j=exp⁡(ai−aj)A_{ij}=\exp(a_{i}-a_{j}). Decompose A​x=tril⁡(A)​x+triu⁡(A)​xAx=\mathrm{tril}(A)\,x+\mathrm{triu}(A)\,x and consider the lower triangular part

yi=∑j≤iexp⁡(aj−ai)​xj=exp⁡(−ai)​∑j≤iexp⁡(aj)​xj.y_{i}\;=\;\sum_{j\leq i}\exp(a_{j}-a_{i})\,x_{j}\;=\;\exp(-a_{i})\sum_{j\leq i}\exp(a_{j})\,x_{j}.

The inner sum si=∑j≤iexp⁡(aj)​xjs_{i}=\sum_{j\leq i}\exp(a_{j})\,x_{j} satisfies the recurrence s1=exp⁡(a1)​x1s_{1}=\exp(a_{1})\,x_{1}, si=si−1+exp⁡(ai)​xis_{i}=s_{i-1}+\exp(a_{i})\,x_{i}. This recurrence is associative, hence parallel: a prefix-scan computes (si)(s_{i}) in 𝒪⁡(n)\mathcal{O}(n) work and 𝒪⁡(log⁡n)\mathcal{O}(\log n) depth, after which yi=exp⁡(−ai)​siy_{i}=\exp(-a_{i})\,s_{i} is a pointwise rescaling. The above scan-based formulation can be implemented as an associative operators on pairs (A,B)(A,B) using the binary operator

(A1,B1)⊕(A2,B2)=(A1+A2,exp⁡(A2)​B1+B2),(A_{1},B_{1})\oplus(A_{2},B_{2})=\left(A_{1}+A_{2},\;\exp(A_{2})\,B_{1}+B_{2}\right),

which is compatible with parallel prefix-scan.

While PyTorch does not provide a native parallel prefix-scan primitive analogous to associative_scan, the prefix computation can be implemented efficiently using logcumsumexp in the log-domain. Starting from

yi=exp⁡(−ai)​∑j≤iexp⁡(aj)​xj,y_{i}=\exp(-a_{i})\sum_{j\leq i}\exp(a_{j})x_{j},

we observe that the sum can be stably computed via a cumulative complex log-sum-exp.

We compute prefix values via

log⁡si=logcumsumexpj≤i​(aj+log⁡xj).\log s_{i}=\texttt{logcumsumexp}_{j\leq i}\!\bigl(a_{j}+\log x_{j}\bigr).

The final result is then obtained as

yi=exp⁡(−ai+log⁡si).y_{i}=\exp(-a_{i}+\log s_{i}).

This approach replaces the explicit prefix-sum with a numerically stable cumulative log-sum-exp, yielding a fully vectorized and GPU-efficient implementation within the standard PyTorch API.

B.2 General case via the shorter axis (n≤kn\leq k)

We now prove the main-text Theorem on the ℝn→ℝk\mathbb{R}^{n}\!\to\!\mathbb{R}^{k} matvec with the kernel A=LAPLEX​(a,b)∈ℝn×kA=\mbox{LAPLEX}(a,b)\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times k} in the regime n≤kn\leq k, and locate its complexity.

Theorem 4 (Reduction via the aa-axis).

Assume a1≤⋯≤ana_{1}\leq\cdots\leq a_{n} and extend with a0=−∞a_{0}=-\infty, an+1=+∞a_{n+1}=+\infty. For i=1,…,n+1i=1,\ldots,n+1 define the intervals

Pi=[ai−1,ai).P_{i}=[a_{i-1},a_{i}).

Given b,x∈ℝkb,x\in\mathbb{R}^{k}, define u,v∈ℝnu,v\in\mathbb{R}^{n} by:

ui=∑j:bj∈Pixjeai−bj,vi=∑j:bj∈Pixjebj−ai.u_{i}=\sum_{j:b_{j}\in P_{i}}x_{j}\,e^{\,a_{i}-b_{j}},\qquad v_{i}=\sum_{j:b_{j}\in P_{i}}x_{j}\,e^{\,b_{j}-a_{i}}.

Let K=LAPLEX​(a)∈ℝn×nK=\mbox{LAPLEX}(a)\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times n} be the kernel matrix with entries Ki​j=e−|ai−aj|K_{ij}=e^{-|a_{i}-a_{j}|}. Then the product y=LAPLEX​(a,b)​xy=\mbox{LAPLEX}(a,b)\,x satisfies

y=triu⁡(K)​u+tril⁡(K)​v,y\;=\;\mathrm{triu}(K)\,u\;+\;\mathrm{tril}(K)\,v,

where triu⁡(K)\mathrm{triu}(K) is the strictly upper-triangular part of KK and tril⁡(K)\mathrm{tril}(K) is the lower-triangular part including the diagonal.

Proof.

By definition,

yi=∑j=1ke−|ai−bj|xj=∑r=1n+1∑j:bj∈Pre−|ai−bj|xj.y_{i}=\sum_{j=1}^{k}e^{-|a_{i}-b_{j}|}\,x_{j}=\sum_{r=1}^{n+1}\;\sum_{j:b_{j}\in P_{r}}e^{-|a_{i}-b_{j}|}\,x_{j}.

We split the outer sum at r=ir=i and analyze the two regions separately.

Region r>ir>i (right of aia_{i}). For bj∈Prb_{j}\in P_{r} with r>ir>i we have bj≥ar−1≥aib_{j}\geq a_{r-1}\geq a_{i}, hence |ai−bj|=bj−ai|a_{i}-b_{j}|=b_{j}-a_{i}. Therefore

e−|ai−bj|=eai−bj=eai−ar​ear−bj.e^{-|a_{i}-b_{j}|}=e^{a_{i}-b_{j}}=e^{a_{i}-a_{r}}\,e^{a_{r}-b_{j}}.

Summing over all jj with bj∈Prb_{j}\in P_{r} yields e−(ar−ai)​ure^{-(a_{r}-a_{i})}\,u_{r}. Summing over all r>ir>i gives

∑r=i+1n+1e−(ar−ai)​ur=∑r>iKi​r​ur=(triu⁡(K)​u)i.\sum_{r=i+1}^{n+1}e^{-(a_{r}-a_{i})}\,u_{r}=\sum_{r>i}K_{ir}\,u_{r}=\bigl(\mathrm{triu}(K)\,u\bigr)_{i}.

Region r≤ir\leq i (left of or at aia_{i}). For bj∈Prb_{j}\in P_{r} with r≤ir\leq i we have bj<ar≤aib_{j}<a_{r}\leq a_{i}, hence |ai−bj|=ai−bj|a_{i}-b_{j}|=a_{i}-b_{j}. Therefore

e−|ai−bj|=ebj−ai=e−(ai−ar)​ebj−ar.e^{-|a_{i}-b_{j}|}=e^{b_{j}-a_{i}}=e^{-(a_{i}-a_{r})}\,e^{b_{j}-a_{r}}.

Summing over all jj with bj∈Prb_{j}\in P_{r} yields e−(ai−ar)​vre^{-(a_{i}-a_{r})}\,v_{r}. Summing over all r≤ir\leq i gives

∑r=1ie−(ai−ar)​vr=∑r≤iKi​r​vr=(tril⁡(K)​v)i.\sum_{r=1}^{i}e^{-(a_{i}-a_{r})}\,v_{r}=\sum_{r\leq i}K_{ir}\,v_{r}=\bigl(\mathrm{tril}(K)\,v\bigr)_{i}.

Adding the two contributions yields yi=(triu⁡(K)​u)i+(tril⁡(K)​v)iy_{i}=(\mathrm{triu}(K)u)_{i}+(\mathrm{tril}(K)v)_{i}, which completes the proof. ∎

Complexity, case n≤kn\leq k.

Sorting aa costs 𝒪⁡(n​log⁡n)\mathcal{O}(n\log n). Each bjb_{j} is placed in its bucket PrP_{r} via binary search, costing 𝒪⁡(k​log⁡n)\mathcal{O}(k\log n) in total. Forming uu and vv from the bucketed contributions is 𝒪⁡(k)\mathcal{O}(k) pointwise work. The two triangular kernel multiplications are 𝒪⁡(n)\mathcal{O}(n) each by Sec. B.1. In total, we have

𝒪⁡(n​log⁡n)+𝒪⁡(k​log​n)+𝒪⁡(k)+𝒪⁡(n)=𝒪⁡(k​log​n)when ​n≤k.\mathcal{O}(n\log n)\;+\;\mathcal{O}(k\log n)\;+\;\mathcal{O}(k)\;+\;\mathcal{O}(n)\;=\;\mathcal{O}(k\log n)\quad\text{when }n\leq k.

If the sort of aa can be cached across multiple matvecs (as in attention or training, where the same anchors are reused over many batches), it amortises away and the per-call cost drops to 𝒪⁡(n+k​log⁡n)=𝒪⁡(k​log⁡n)\mathcal{O}(n+k\log n)=\mathcal{O}(k\log n).

B.3 Dual reduction via the shorter axis (n≥kn\geq k)

In the regime n≥kn\geq k the symmetric construction operates on bb rather than aa: we sort bb, scan the symmetric kernel LAPLEX​(b)\mbox{LAPLEX}(b) over bb, and propagate the result to each aia_{i} by a binary search and a pair of pointwise products.

Theorem 5 (Dual reduction via the bb-axis).

Assume b1≤⋯≤bkb_{1}\leq\cdots\leq b_{k} and let K=LAPLEX​(b)K=\mbox{LAPLEX}(b). Define

u=tril⁡(K)​x,v=triu⁡(K)​x.u\;=\;\mathrm{tril}(K)\,x,\qquad v\;=\;\mathrm{triu}(K)\,x.

For each ii, set ji=max⁡{j:bj≤ai}j_{i}=\max\{j:b_{j}\leq a_{i}\}, with ji=0j_{i}=0 if no such jj exists. Then y=LAPLEX​(a,b)​xy=\mbox{LAPLEX}(a,b)\,x satisfies

yi={exp⁡(bji−ai)​ujiji≥1,0otherwise,+{exp⁡(ai−bji+1)​vji+1ji<k,0otherwise.y_{i}\;=\;\begin{cases}\exp(b_{j_{i}}-a_{i})\,u_{j_{i}}&j_{i}\geq 1,\\ 0&\text{otherwise},\end{cases}\;+\;\begin{cases}\exp(a_{i}-b_{j_{i}+1})\,v_{j_{i}+1}&j_{i}<k,\\ 0&\text{otherwise}.\end{cases}
Proof.

Fix ii and split the sum at the threshold jij_{i}

yi=∑j≤jiexp⁡(bj−ai)​xj+∑j>jiexp⁡(ai−bj)​xj.y_{i}\;=\;\sum_{j\leq j_{i}}\exp(b_{j}-a_{i})\,x_{j}\;+\;\sum_{j>j_{i}}\exp(a_{i}-b_{j})\,x_{j}.

Factoring out the dependence on aia_{i} we have

yi=exp⁡(−ai)​∑j≤jiexp⁡(bj)​xj+exp⁡(ai)​∑j>jiexp⁡(−bj)​xj.y_{i}\;=\;\exp(-a_{i})\sum_{j\leq j_{i}}\exp(b_{j})\,x_{j}\;+\;\exp(a_{i})\sum_{j>j_{i}}\exp(-b_{j})\,x_{j}.

The triangular kernel applied to bb yields

uj=∑l≤jexp⁡(bl−bj)​xl,vj=∑l≥jexp⁡(bj−bl)​xl,u_{j}=\sum_{l\leq j}\exp(b_{l}-b_{j})\,x_{l},\qquad v_{j}=\sum_{l\geq j}\exp(b_{j}-b_{l})\,x_{l},

what, after multiplying both sides by exp⁡(bj)\exp(b_{j}) and exp⁡(−bj)\exp(-b_{j}) gives

∑l≤jexp⁡(bl)​xl=exp⁡(bj)​uj,∑l≥jexp⁡(−bl)​xl=exp⁡(−bj)​vj.\sum_{l\leq j}\exp(b_{l})\,x_{l}=\exp(b_{j})\,u_{j},\qquad\sum_{l\geq j}\exp(-b_{l})\,x_{l}=\exp(-b_{j})\,v_{j}.

Evaluating these identities at j=jij=j_{i} and j=ji+1j=j_{i}+1 gives the desired formula. ∎

Complexity, case n≥kn\geq k.

Sort of bb costs 𝒪⁡(k​log⁡k)\mathcal{O}(k\log k); the two triangular kernel multiplications cost 𝒪⁡(k)\mathcal{O}(k) via the symmetric scan. Each of the nn split points jij_{i} is found by binary search in 𝒪⁡(log⁡k)\mathcal{O}(\log k), giving 𝒪⁡(n​log⁡k)\mathcal{O}(n\log k) total. Final evaluation of yy is 𝒪⁡(n)\mathcal{O}(n). Adding the components,

𝒪⁡(k​log⁡k)+𝒪⁡(k)+𝒪⁡(n​log​k)+𝒪⁡(n)=𝒪⁡(n​log​k)when ​n≥k.\mathcal{O}(k\log k)\;+\;\mathcal{O}(k)\;+\;\mathcal{O}(n\log k)\;+\;\mathcal{O}(n)\;=\;\mathcal{O}(n\log k)\quad\text{when }n\geq k.

As before, the sort of bb amortises away when the same anchors are reused.

B.4 Combined complexity

Combining both branches, the implementation dispatches automatically on min⁡(n,k)\min(n,k):

TLAPLEX​(n,k)=𝒪⁡(max⁡(n,k)​log⁡min⁡(n,k))\boxed{\quad T_{\mbox{LAPLEX}}(n,k)\;=\;\mathcal{O}\bigl(\max(n,k)\,\log\min(n,k)\bigr)\quad}

for a single matrix–vector product, against the 𝒪⁡(n​k)\mathcal{O}(nk) of the dense baseline. In a batch of BB vectors sharing the same anchors, the sort and the binary-search results are reused across the batch, and the per-vector cost drops to

TLAPLEX​(n,k,B)=𝒪⁡(B​max⁡(n,k)​log⁡min⁡(n,k))+𝒪⁡(max⁡(n,k)​log⁡min⁡(n,k)).T_{\mbox{LAPLEX}}(n,k,B)\;=\;\mathcal{O}\bigl(B\,\max(n,k)\,\log\min(n,k)\bigr)\;+\;\mathcal{O}\bigl(\max(n,k)\log\min(n,k)\bigr).

Memory usage is 𝒪⁡(B⁡(n+k))\mathcal{O}(B(n+k)) for the working tensors, with no n×kn\!\times\!k matrix ever materialized.

Appendix C Fast weighted Gram matrix: proof and complexity

The matrix–vector reductions explain how to apply a single Laplace operator. The weighted Gram result is the next step: it shows that the same one-dimensional ordering also controls the second-order object that appears in kernel methods, curvature approximations, and Woodbury likelihoods. We prove the main-text theorem for

M=A​diag​(D)​A⊤,Ai​j=exp⁡(−|ai−bj|),D∈ℝ+k,M\;=\;A\,\mathrm{diag}(D)\,A^{\!\top},\qquad A_{ij}\;=\;\exp(-|a_{i}-b_{j}|),\qquad D\in\mathbb{R}^{k}_{+},

in 𝒪⁡(n2+k​log⁡n)\mathcal{O}(n^{2}+k\log n) rather than the 𝒪⁡(n2​k)\mathcal{O}(n^{2}k) of the naive matmul (see Fig. 7).

Theorem 6 (Exact Gram decomposition).

Let a1≤⋯≤ana_{1}\leq\cdots\leq a_{n}, and set a0=−∞a_{0}=-\infty, an+1=+∞a_{n+1}=+\infty. Partition ℝ\mathbb{R} into intervals

Pr:=[ar−1,ar),r=1,…,n.P_{r}:=[a_{r-1},a_{r}),\qquad r=1,\dots,n.

Given b∈ℝkb\in\mathbb{R}^{k} and weights D∈ℝkD\in\mathbb{R}^{k}, define u,v,w∈ℝnu,v,w\in\mathbb{R}^{n} by

ui:=∑bt∈Pie2​(bt−ai)​Dt,vi:=∑bt∈Pie2​(ai−bt)​Dt,wi:=∑bt∈PiDt.u_{i}:=\sum_{b_{t}\in P_{i}}e^{2(b_{t}-a_{i})}\,D_{t},\qquad v_{i}:=\sum_{b_{t}\in P_{i}}e^{2(a_{i}-b_{t})}\,D_{t},\qquad w_{i}:=\sum_{b_{t}\in P_{i}}D_{t}.

Let Wi:=∑r≤iwrW_{i}:=\sum_{r\leq i}w_{r} be the cumulative weights. Define the kernel matrix K∈ℝn×nK\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times n} by Ki​j:=e−2​|ai−aj|K_{ij}:=e^{-2|a_{i}-a_{j}|}, and let A:=LAPLEX​(a,b)A:=\mbox{LAPLEX}(a,b). Set additionally

U:=tril⁡(K)​u,V:=triu⁡(K)​v.U:=\operatorname{tril}(K)\,u,\qquad V:=\operatorname{triu}(K)\,v.

Then the Gram matrix M:=A​diag⁡(D)​A⊤M:=A\,\operatorname{diag}(D)\,A^{\top} satisfies, for all i≥ji\geq j,

Mi​j=eaj−ai​(Uj+(Wi−Wj)+Vi),M_{ij}=e^{a_{j}-a_{i}}\,\bigl(U_{j}+(W_{i}-W_{j})+V_{i}\bigr),

with symmetry Mj​i=Mi​jM_{ji}=M_{ij}.

Proof.

By definition, Mi​j=∑t=1NDt​e−|ai−bt|​e−|aj−bt|M_{ij}=\sum_{t=1}^{N}D_{t}\,e^{-|a_{i}-b_{t}|}\,e^{-|a_{j}-b_{t}|}, and assume i≥ji\geq j. We partition the inner sum into three disjoint regions according to the position of btb_{t} relative to aja_{j} and aia_{i}.

Left region (bt≤ajb_{t}\leq a_{j}). Here bt≤aj≤aib_{t}\leq a_{j}\leq a_{i}, so |ai−bt|=ai−bt|a_{i}-b_{t}|=a_{i}-b_{t} and |aj−bt|=aj−bt|a_{j}-b_{t}|=a_{j}-b_{t}. Hence

e−|ai−bt|​e−|aj−bt|=e−(ai−bt)​e−(aj−bt)=e−(ai+aj)​e2​bt.e^{-|a_{i}-b_{t}|}e^{-|a_{j}-b_{t}|}=e^{-(a_{i}-b_{t})}e^{-(a_{j}-b_{t})}=e^{-(a_{i}+a_{j})}e^{2b_{t}}.

Summing over all bt≤ajb_{t}\leq a_{j} (i.e., over intervals PrP_{r} with r≤jr\leq j) yields

e−(ai+aj)​∑r≤j∑bt∈PrDt​e2​bt=e−(ai+aj)​∑r≤je2​ar​ur.e^{-(a_{i}+a_{j})}\sum_{r\leq j}\sum_{b_{t}\in P_{r}}D_{t}e^{2b_{t}}=e^{-(a_{i}+a_{j})}\sum_{r\leq j}e^{2a_{r}}u_{r}.

By definition, Uj=∑r≤jKj​r​ur=∑r≤je−2​(aj−ar)​ur=e−2​aj​∑r≤je2​ar​urU_{j}=\sum_{r\leq j}K_{jr}u_{r}=\sum_{r\leq j}e^{-2(a_{j}-a_{r})}u_{r}=e^{-2a_{j}}\sum_{r\leq j}e^{2a_{r}}u_{r}. Thus the left contribution simplifies to eaj−ai​Uje^{a_{j}-a_{i}}U_{j}.

Middle region (aj<bt≤aia_{j}<b_{t}\leq a_{i}). Here |ai−bt|=ai−bt|a_{i}-b_{t}|=a_{i}-b_{t} and |aj−bt|=bt−aj|a_{j}-b_{t}|=b_{t}-a_{j}. The product becomes

e−(ai−bt)​e−(bt−aj)=e−(ai−aj)=eaj−ai,e^{-(a_{i}-b_{t})}e^{-(b_{t}-a_{j})}=e^{-(a_{i}-a_{j})}=e^{a_{j}-a_{i}},

which is independent of btb_{t}. Summing over this region gives

eaj−ai​∑aj<bt≤aiDt=eaj−ai​(Wi−Wj).e^{a_{j}-a_{i}}\sum_{a_{j}<b_{t}\leq a_{i}}D_{t}=e^{a_{j}-a_{i}}(W_{i}-W_{j}).

Right region (bt>aib_{t}>a_{i}). Here bt>ai≥ajb_{t}>a_{i}\geq a_{j}, so |ai−bt|=bt−ai|a_{i}-b_{t}|=b_{t}-a_{i} and |aj−bt|=bt−aj|a_{j}-b_{t}|=b_{t}-a_{j}. Hence

e−|ai−bt|​e−|aj−bt|=e−(bt−ai)​e−(bt−aj)=eai+aj​e−2​bt.e^{-|a_{i}-b_{t}|}e^{-|a_{j}-b_{t}|}=e^{-(b_{t}-a_{i})}e^{-(b_{t}-a_{j})}=e^{a_{i}+a_{j}}e^{-2b_{t}}.

Summing over all bt>aib_{t}>a_{i} (intervals PrP_{r} with r>ir>i) yields

eai+aj​∑r>i∑bt∈PrDt​e−2​bt=eai+aj​∑r>ie−2​ar​vr.e^{a_{i}+a_{j}}\sum_{r>i}\sum_{b_{t}\in P_{r}}D_{t}e^{-2b_{t}}=e^{a_{i}+a_{j}}\sum_{r>i}e^{-2a_{r}}v_{r}.

Using Vi=∑r>iKi​r​vr=∑r>ie−2​(ar−ai)​vr=e2​ai​∑r>ie−2​ar​vrV_{i}=\sum_{r>i}K_{ir}v_{r}=\sum_{r>i}e^{-2(a_{r}-a_{i})}v_{r}=e^{2a_{i}}\sum_{r>i}e^{-2a_{r}}v_{r}, the right contribution simplifies to eaj−ai​Vie^{a_{j}-a_{i}}V_{i}.

Adding the three contributions and factoring out eaj−aie^{a_{j}-a_{i}} yields the claimed formula. Symmetry Mj​i=Mi​jM_{ji}=M_{ij} follows directly from the definition of MM and the absolute value in the exponent. ∎

Complexity.

Sorting aa and bucketing bb cost 𝒪⁡(n​log⁡n+k​log⁡n)\mathcal{O}(n\log n+k\log n). The per-interval aggregates pi,si,wip_{i},s_{i},w_{i} are each a one-pass scatter over bb, 𝒪⁡(k)\mathcal{O}(k). The cumulative quantities Pi,Si,WiP_{i},S_{i},W_{i} are prefix scans, 𝒪⁡(n)\mathcal{O}(n). Once P,S,WP,S,W are tabulated, each entry Mi​jM_{ij} is evaluated in 𝒪⁡(1)\mathcal{O}(1) from the boxed formula, so the dominant cost is the explicit construction of the n×nn\times n matrix:

TGram(n,k)=𝒪(n2+klogn),\boxed{\quad T_{\mathrm{Gram}}(n,k)\;=\;\mathcal{O}\bigl(n^{2}+k\log n\bigr),\quad}

versus 𝒪⁡(n2​k)\mathcal{O}(n^{2}k) for the dense reference. The Θ⁡(n2)\Theta(n^{2}) component is the size of the output matrix and is unavoidable. The asymptotic speed-up over the dense baseline is Θ⁡(n2​k/(n2+k​log⁡n))\Theta(n^{2}\,k/(n^{2}+k\log n)), which reduces to Θ⁡(k/log⁡n)\Theta(k/\log n) when k​log⁡n≳n2k\log n\gtrsim n^{2} and to Θ⁡(k)\Theta(k) when the inner dimension dominates. Memory is 𝒪⁡(n2+k)\mathcal{O}(n^{2}+k), again dominated by the output.

Appendix D Kernel-algebra benchmarks: full empirical record

The main text compresses the kernel-algebra story into one central figure. Here we unpack it into the individual stress tests behind Sec. 4.1. We benchmark the three kernel-algebra primitives provided by LAPLEX: matrix–vector multiplication X​K​(a,b)X\,K(a,b) (and its transpose), and the weighted Gram matrix K⁡(α,β)​diag​(D)​K​(α,β)⊤K(\alpha,\beta)\,\mathrm{diag}(D)\,K(\alpha,\beta)^{\!\top}, where K​(a,b)i​j=exp⁡(−|ai−bj|)K(a,b)_{ij}=\exp(-|a_{i}-b_{j}|). Each timing is the best of three independent runs of 3030 timed iterations after 1010 warm-up iterations, with explicit cuda.synchronize() barriers around the timed region. For backward measurements we form ℒ=𝟏⊤​Y\mathcal{L}=\mathbf{1}^{\!\top}\!Y with YY the operator output and back-propagate through the inputs (data tensor and both anchor sets). The explicit-dense baseline materializes the full n×kn\times k kernel matrix and uses a single torch.matmul call; this is the strongest PyTorch baseline whenever memory permits. We report a baseline measurement only as long as it does not exceed either a 500500 ms wall-clock budget or a 1.51.5 GB VRAM allocation estimate; once either threshold trips, every larger problem size for the baseline is marked OOM and shown as a vertical dashed line on the corresponding plot.

D.1 GPU runtime, peak memory, and forward+backward

Setup.

Square kernel (n=kn=k), batch size B=8B=8. We sweep n∈{210,211,…,220}n\in\{2^{10},2^{11},\dots,2^{20}\} for LAPLEX and n∈{210,…,214}n\in\{2^{10},\dots,2^{14}\} for the explicit-dense baseline; at n=215n=2^{15} the dense KK matrix already exceeds 22 GB and the forward+backward graph triggers an OOM on this hardware.

Observations.

The forward time of LAPLEX grows roughly linearly between n=217n=2^{17} and n=220n=2^{20} (consistent with the 𝒪⁡(B⁡(n+k))\mathcal{O}(B(n+k)) working set, dominated by memory bandwidth at these sizes), while sub-n=217n=2^{17} measurements are dominated by constant kernel-launch overhead and stay flat at ∼1\sim\!1 ms, (see Fig. 8). The forward+backward time is approximately 3×3\times the forward time (one extra scan launch plus the fused ∂/∂α\partial/\partial\alpha reduction), independent of nn. Peak memory grows as 𝒪⁡(B​n)\mathcal{O}(Bn) with a small constant (the working set is the input tensor plus a few (B,n)(B,n) scratch buffers), and at n=220n=2^{20} uses ∼320\sim\!320 MB. The dense baseline uses 𝒪⁡(n2)\mathcal{O}(n^{2}) memory and OOMs at the very small problem size of n=215=32​Kn=2^{15}=32\text{K}.

D.2 Numerical accuracy

Setup.

We compare LAPLEX’s float32 forward output and the explicit float32 dense matmul both against an float64 dense ground truth. The same input tensors a,b,Xa,b,X in float32 are cast to float64 for the reference; the difference therefore reflects only the algorithmic precision of the two float32 routes, not input rounding. Square kernel, B=8B=8, n∈{210,…,214}n\in\{2^{10},\dots,2^{14}\}.

Observations.

Although LAPLEX’s float32 path uses an internally rescaled mantissa–exponent representation, its output relative error is lower than that of the corresponding X​@​KX@K matmul performed in the same precision. This is intuitive: the explicit dense path must sum nn terms of comparable magnitude in a single accumulator, picking up an O⁡(n​ε)O(n\,\varepsilon) rounding error that grows visibly with nn, while the decoupled-lookback scan in LAPLEX introduces a single ε\varepsilon per element. At all tested sizes the ℓ∞\ell_{\infty} error of LAPLEX stays below 5⋅10−75\cdot 10^{-7}, and the ℓ2\ell_{2} error stays at ∼1.5⋅10−7\sim\!1.5\cdot 10^{-7} (see Fig. 9).

D.3 Batch-size scaling

Setup.

We fix n=k=214n=k=2^{14} and sweep B∈{1,2,4,…,28}B\in\{1,2,4,\dots,2^{8}\}. For the explicit-dense baseline, the forward+backward graph (which retains the 11 GB matrix KK) triggers OOM for B>32B>32 on this hardware; those entries are reported as OOM.

Observations.

The dense baseline’s runtime is essentially the cost of forming the n×nn\times n kernel matrix; the subsequent X​@​KX@K matmul is so inexpensive next to that operation that batch size has very little effect. This pattern flips for LAPLEX: there is no KK to form, so the cost is entirely 𝒪⁡(B⋅n)\mathcal{O}(B\cdot n) in the small-BB regime and remains so up to B=256B=256. The crossover where LAPLEX starts showing batch dependence is at B≈8B\approx 8; below that, kernel-launch overhead dominates. The baseline’s apparent dense-fb plateau at ∼1.4\sim\!1.4 s is purely the time of computing the gradient of the explicit kernel matrix construction – a cost that LAPLEX sidesteps entirely (see Fig. 10).

D.4 Asymmetric kernels: fixed short axis

Setup.

The 𝒪⁡(n​log⁡n+k)\mathcal{O}(n\log n+k) scan-based algorithm we use selects the shorter axis automatically: when n≤kn\leq k it scans along aa and gathers per bb (branch A), otherwise it scatters from aa into buckets along sorted bb and scans along bb (branch B). Both branches share the same asymptotic cost but expose different sets of operations. We test each branch with the corresponding axis fixed at 10241024 and the other swept across {210,211,…,220}\{2^{10},2^{11},\dots,2^{20}\}.

Observations.

With n=1024n=1024 fixed, LAPLEX’s forward stays under 1.11.1 ms up to k=217k=2^{17} and only reaches 77 ms at k=220k=2^{20}; the dense baseline reaches 9191 ms at k=218k=2^{18} before OOM-ing. The mirror-image experiment (k=1024k=1024 fixed, nn varying) shows nearly identical behavior with a slight overhead from the scatter-add step. At the maximum tested size with the dense baseline still running (nn or k=218k=2^{18}), LAPLEX delivers ∼37\sim\!37–47×47\times speed-up; both implementations of the dense baseline OOM at 2192^{19} (see Fig. 11).

D.5 Weighted Gram matrix

Setup.

For the weighted-Gram operation M=K⁡(α,β)​diag​(D)​K​(α,β)⊤M=K(\alpha,\beta)\,\mathrm{diag}(D)\,K(\alpha,\beta)^{\!\top} we fix the output dimension at n=1024n=1024 (so the result MM is always a 1024×10241024\times 1024 matrix, 44 MB in float32) and sweep the inner dimension k∈{210,…,220}k\in\{2^{10},\dots,2^{20}\}. This isolates the algorithmic scaling: we want to measure how the cost depends on the dimension we sum over, not on the size of the result.

Observations.

The flat plateau in the forward-time panel is the predicted behavior of the algorithm. Working backwards from the analytical cost 𝒪⁡(n2+k​log⁡n)\mathcal{O}(n^{2}+k\log n): the n2n^{2} term is 10242≈1061024^{2}\approx 10^{6} FLOPs and dominates until the inner-dimension term k​log⁡n=10​kk\log n=10\,k catches up around k≈105k\approx 10^{5}, at which point LAPLEX begins to grow linearly in kk. The dense baseline is 𝒪⁡(n2​k)\mathcal{O}(n^{2}k) in time and uses 𝒪⁡(n​k)\mathcal{O}(nk) memory, so its time grows linearly with kk and so does its memory; at the last non-OOM measurement k=217k=2^{17} it costs 216216 ms (LAPLEX: 1.451.45 ms, 149×149\times speed-up) and uses 1.01.0 GB of VRAM (LAPLEX: 3333 MB, see Fig. 12).

Asymptotic speed-up.

For any fixed nn, the dense Gram costs 𝒪⁡(n2​k)\mathcal{O}(n^{2}k) while LAPLEX costs 𝒪⁡(n2+k​log⁡n)=𝒪⁡(max⁡(n2,k​log⁡n))\mathcal{O}(n^{2}+k\log n)=\mathcal{O}(\max(n^{2},k\log n)). In the regime where the inner dimension dominates (k​log⁡n≫n2k\log n\gg n^{2}), the speed-up of LAPLEX over the dense baseline is asymptotically Θ⁡(n2/log⁡n)\Theta(n^{2}/\log n).

D.6 CPU benchmark (no CUDA backend)

Setup.

The LAPLEX package ships with a portable pure-PyTorch implementation (laplex_noCUDA) built on a single torch.logcumsumexp call per scan; this version supports CPU, CUDA, MPS, and ROCm uniformly and requires no compilation. We benchmark it on CPU only, so the custom CUDA path is not invoked. Square kernel, B=1B=1, n∈{210,…,214}n\in\{2^{10},\dots,2^{14}\}.

Observations.

The pure-PyTorch path is intentionally several times slower than the custom CUDA backend on a per-call basis (compare the ∼1\sim\!1 ms-at-n=214n=2^{14} figure of Section D.1 against the ∼6\sim\!6 ms here), but it is portable to any device PyTorch supports and requires no compilation step on first import. The dense baseline’s CPU time grows from 0.70.7 ms at n=210n=2^{10} to 662662 ms at n=214n=2^{14}, putting the speed-up of even the pure-PyTorch LAPLEX over 100×100\times at the largest tested size and making it the only path of the two that is usable for moderate-nn kernel work without a GPU (see Fig. 13).

D.7 Summary of empirical findings

Across all six stress tests, the same pattern repeats: avoiding the explicit kernel matrix is not just an asymptotic win, but a practical wall-clock and memory win on commodity hardware. Concretely:

  • •

    On GPU at the largest size where the dense baseline still runs (n=k=214n=k=2^{14}, B=8B=8), LAPLEX is ∼65×\sim\!65\times faster on the forward pass, ∼430×\sim\!430\times faster on forward+backward, and uses ∼100×\sim\!100\times less peak VRAM (Sec. D.1).

  • •

    LAPLEX scales gracefully far past the OOM point of the dense baseline: at n=220n=2^{20}, the forward+backward call takes ∼71\sim\!71 ms and uses ∼320\sim\!320 MB of VRAM (Sec. D.1).

  • •

    Despite running internally in float32, LAPLEX delivers better relative-error numbers than the explicit dense float32 matmul against an float64 ground truth, at all tested nn (Sec. D.2).

  • •

    For asymmetric workloads with a short axis fixed at 10241024, LAPLEX gives ∼37\sim\!37–47×47\times speed-up at the last non-OOM point of the dense baseline (Sec. D.4).

  • •

    The weighted-Gram operation enjoys an asymptotic Θ⁡(n2/log⁡n)\Theta(n^{2}/\log n) speed-up over the dense baseline, with 149×149\times measured at the largest non-OOM size (n=1024n=1024, k=217k=2^{17}; Sec. D.5).

  • •

    Even on CPU, the pure-PyTorch reference implementation is already 108×108\times faster than the explicit dense matmul at n=214n=2^{14} (Sec. D.6).

These measurements are the empirical backbone for the main-text claim that LAPLEX behaves like a fast transform in practice while retaining exact Laplace-kernel semantics.

Appendix E FFT and Toeplitz–FFT baselines: full comparison

This appendix section spells out the relationship between LAPLEX and FFT-based multiplication. The important structural fact is simple: Toeplitz–FFT is the uniform-grid specialization of the Laplace operator studied in this paper. If ai=bi=i​Δa_{i}=b_{i}=i\Delta, then LAPLEX​(a,b)\mbox{LAPLEX}(a,b) is a Toeplitz matrix and circulant embedding gives an exact FFT-based matvec. If the anchors are irregular or learned, that diagonalization disappears. The experiments below therefore measure the cost and benefit of leaving the fixed-grid slice.

We separate four questions: runtime on GPU, accuracy on the uniform-grid case where Toeplitz–FFT is exactly applicable, runtime without a custom GPU kernel, and differentiability with respect to anchor locations. This is the comparison that matters for a learnable fast transform: FFT methods provide the best constants on their slice, while LAPLEX keeps the same asymptotic class on a strictly larger and trainable family.

E.1 GPU runtime (recap)

Figure 14 reports single-vector (B=1B=1) wall-clock times for LAPLEX, Toeplitz–FFT, and a single cuFFT call across n∈{210,…,220}n\in\{2^{10},\dots,2^{20}\}. All three curves are parallel on a log–log plot with slope ≈n​log⁡n\approx n\log n, confirming the matching asymptotic complexity class. This behaviour is further corroborated by Fig. 15, which extends the analysis to larger problem sizes and additionally reports memory usage, showing consistent scaling trends across architectures. The constant-factor breakdown is LAPLEX:Toeplitz–FFT:cuFFT≈4:1:0.13\mbox{LAPLEX}{}:\text{Toeplitz--FFT}:\text{cuFFT}\approx 4:1:0.13 at n=220n=2^{20}, i.e. LAPLEX is ∼4×\sim\!4\times slower than the specialised circulant-embedding code, which itself is ∼8×\sim\!8\times slower than a single (non-multiplying) cuFFT call – a ratio that simply reflects the fact that Toeplitz–FFT performs three FFTs on a vector of length 2​n2n plus a pointwise multiplication and a padding operation. The crucial observation is that all three have the same slope on the log–log plot.

E.2 Numerical accuracy on a uniform-grid (Toeplitz) problem

Setup.

We pick uniform anchors ai=bi=i​Δa_{i}=b_{i}=i\Delta with Δ=1/n\Delta=1/n, so the kernel matrix K​(a,b)i​j=exp⁡(−|i−j|​Δ)K(a,b)_{ij}\!=\!\exp(-|i-j|\Delta) is symmetric Toeplitz and Toeplitz–FFT is exactly applicable. X∈ℝB×nX\!\in\!\mathbb{R}^{B\times n} is sampled 𝒩⁡(0,1)\mathcal{N}(0,1) in float32. We compute X​KXK via four routes: (i) dense float64 (the ground truth); (ii) dense float32 matmul; (iii) Toeplitz–FFT float32 (circulant embedding + 3×3\times FFT); (iv) LAPLEX float32 (prefix/suffix scan). We report the relative ℓ2\ell_{2} and ℓ∞\ell_{\infty} errors of routes (ii)–(iv) against the (i) reference, B=8B=8, n∈{210,…,214}n\in\{2^{10},\dots,2^{14}\}.

Observations.

At n=214n=2^{14} the relative ℓ∞\ell_{\infty} errors are dense fp32≈1.1⋅10−6\text{dense fp32}\!\approx\!1.1\cdot 10^{-6}, Toeplitz–FFT≈4.4⋅10−7\text{Toeplitz--FFT}\!\approx\!4.4\cdot 10^{-7}, LAPLEX≈4.2⋅10−7\mbox{LAPLEX}{}\!\approx\!4.2\cdot 10^{-7} (see Fig. 16). Three remarks.

(a) The dense float32 matmul accumulates 𝒪⁡(n​ε)\mathcal{O}(n\,\varepsilon) rounding error, visible as the upward-tilting orange curve. Both fast methods avoid this accumulation.

(b) Toeplitz–FFT inherits the well-known 𝒪⁡(log⁡n⋅ε)\mathcal{O}(\log n\cdot\varepsilon) accuracy of a butterfly FFT plus a small extra constant from the complex-valued IFFT and from the single pointwise multiplication; the result is roughly flat in nn and noticeably better than dense float32.

(c) LAPLEX keeps the mantissa–exponent representation in float32 and combines partial sums with 𝒪⁡(ε)\mathcal{O}(\varepsilon) rounding per element, giving an essentially nn-independent error that is even slightly smaller than that of Toeplitz–FFT. Although the asymptotic constant is favorable to FFT (no complex arithmetic in intermediate accumulators), our integer-exponent rescaling means we never accumulate values whose magnitudes differ by many orders of magnitude. This is what makes LAPLEX’s float32 error lower than Toeplitz–FFT’s at all tested sizes.

We emphasise that this experiment is a fair comparison on FFT’s home turf: a uniform grid is exactly the configuration where Toeplitz–FFT is applicable as a baseline. On a non-uniform grid the FFT-based comparator simply does not run.

E.3 CPU runtime (no GPU required)

Setup.

The equal-complexity-class claim of Section 6 relies on the custom CUDA scan compiled by prefix_suffix.py. A natural worry is that the conclusion may change once that specialised kernel is unavailable. This experiment puts that worry to rest: we run all three methods on CPU using only PyTorch built-ins (torch.logcumsumexp for LAPLEX, torch.fft for the FFT baselines), B=1B=1, float32, n∈{210,…,218}n\in\{2^{10},\dots,2^{18}\}.

Observations.

At n=218n=2^{18} the wall-clock costs are LAPLEX≈64\mbox{LAPLEX}{}\!\approx\!64 ms, Toeplitz–FFT≈6\!\approx\!6 ms, torch.fft.fft≈0.65\!\approx\!0.65 ms. The constants on CPU are larger than on GPU, but the scaling pattern is identical to Figure 14: three parallel lines on the log–log plot, with constant-factor ratios LAPLEX:Toeplitz–FFT:FFT≈100:9:1\mbox{LAPLEX}{}:\text{Toeplitz--FFT}:\text{FFT}\approx 100:9:1 at the largest tested size. Notably, while LAPLEX pays a ∼10×\sim\!10\times constant penalty over Toeplitz–FFT on CPU (compared to ∼4×\sim\!4\times on GPU), the dependence on nn is the same on both devices, so the relative cost is bounded above by a constant for any problem size.

The wider gap on CPU is mostly a property of PyTorch’s torch.logcumsumexp, which is single-threaded and not as heavily optimized as the MKL-backed FFT. The gap shrinks substantially on GPU (where our custom CUDA kernel beats a generic primitive) and is therefore a property of the reference implementation in laplex_noCUDA.py, not of the algorithm itself (see Fig. 17).

E.4 Differentiability with respect to the anchor sets

A subtler difference between LAPLEX and the FFT-based baselines is that the FFT path supports gradients only with respect to the input vector, not with respect to the anchor positions themselves. This is intrinsic, not an oversight: the Toeplitz structure is built from a fixed grid spacing Δ\Delta rather than an explicit pair of tensors (a,b)(a,b), so there is nothing “differentiable” on the anchor side. In the language of torch.autograd, attempting loss.backward() with a.requires_grad_(True) returns None or a zero gradient, depending on how the grid spacing was constructed.

This category-level difference is summarized in Table 3 and matters in any setting where the anchors are themselves trainable parameters: feature lookup tables, node embeddings in graph kernel methods, kernel temperature parameters, or end-to-end-trained Gaussian process models. The Toeplitz–FFT comparator is simply unavailable in those settings.

E.5 Other 𝒪⁡(n​log⁡n)\mathcal{O}(n\log n) comparators

For completeness we briefly mention two further fast comparators that do not appear in our benchmark, and explain why.

Non-uniform FFT (NUFFT).

The non-uniform FFT [16, 8] extends the FFT to irregular grids in 𝒪⁡(n​log⁡n)\mathcal{O}(n\log n) time, but only for Fourier-type kernels of the form exp⁡(2​π​i​ai​bj)\exp(2\pi i\,a_{i}\,b_{j}). The Laplace kernel exp⁡(−|ai−bj|)\exp(-|a_{i}-b_{j}|) is not in this family, so NUFFT is not directly applicable: it would require approximating the Laplace decay by a finite Fourier series with bounded support, which loses the smooth tail and reduces the resulting matrix–vector product to a multi-pole expansion (see below). NUFFT is therefore the right tool for kernels where the FFT spectrum is the natural representation, but not for the operator we study.

Fast Multipole Method (FMM) and Hierarchical Semi-Separable matrices.

The 1-D Laplace kernel falls within the broad class to which the Fast Multipole Method [15] and Hierarchically Semi-Separable matrix representations [34] apply. In principle these methods achieve 𝒪⁡(n​log⁡n)\mathcal{O}(n\log n) matvec on irregular grids by hierarchical low-rank factorization of off-diagonal blocks. Modern, PyTorch-friendly, GPU-accelerated, and differentiable FMM implementations for the Laplace kernel are not, to our knowledge, publicly available, and recreating one is a non-trivial software project orthogonal to the contribution of this paper. The advantage of LAPLEX’s scan-based decomposition is that it is mechanically simple, end-to-end differentiable, and exact (within float32 rounding) by construction; FMM is more general (arbitrary smooth kernels) but achieves 𝒪⁡(n​log⁡n)\mathcal{O}(n\log n) only through controlled approximation, with an accuracy/cost trade-off that is non-trivial to tune.

E.6 Summary

The FFT comparison is best summarized as a containment statement plus a constant-factor measurement. Uniform-grid Laplace Toeplitz multiplication is a special case of LAPLEX evaluated by a highly optimized FFT route. LAPLEX pays a moderate constant factor to move from that fixed slice to arbitrary trainable anchors, while preserving exactness and improving float32 accuracy in the tested Toeplitz setting.

  • •

    Same asymptotic class. On GPU (Sec. E.1) and CPU (Sec. E.3), LAPLEX, Toeplitz–FFT, and a single FFT call follow parallel 𝒪⁡(n​log⁡n)\mathcal{O}(n\log n) curves.

  • •

    Special-case constants. Toeplitz–FFT is faster because it assumes a uniform grid and uses a circulant embedding. LAPLEX is slower by a bounded constant but accepts arbitrary anchors and can train them.

  • •

    Numerical accuracy. On the uniform-grid problem where Toeplitz–FFT is valid, LAPLEX gives lower relative float32 error than both dense matmul and Toeplitz–FFT (Sec. E.2).

  • •

    Differentiability. Toeplitz–FFT has no gradients with respect to arbitrary anchor locations, because those locations are not model parameters in the FFT formulation. LAPLEX differentiates through values and anchors.

  • •

    Other comparators. NUFFT targets Fourier-type kernels, not the Laplace kernel directly; FMM/HSS methods are broader but approximate and lack a standard differentiable GPU implementation for this setting (Sec. E.5).

Appendix F Random Fourier Features: value and gradient behavior

RFF is the natural irregular-grid comparator because it approximates the same shift-invariant Laplace kernel without requiring a uniform grid. The comparison is therefore not between unrelated models. It is between an exact ordered-kernel algorithm (LAPLEX) and a finite Monte Carlo factorization of the same kernel (RFF). This section shows why that distinction becomes decisive when the anchor locations are learnable: value errors shrink slowly with the feature count, while anchor-gradient errors inherit the heavy tails of the Cauchy spectral density.

F.1 Setup and value accuracy

The estimator.

Random Fourier Features [23] approximate a shift-invariant kernel k⁡(u−v)k(u-v) via Bochner’s theorem: if pp is the spectral density of kk, then k⁡(u−v)=𝔼w∼p​ei​w​(u−v)=𝔼w∼p,c∼𝒰⁡[0,2​π]​ 2​cos⁡(w​u+c)​cos⁡(w​v+c)k(u-v)=\mathbb{E}_{w\sim p}\,e^{iw(u-v)}=\mathbb{E}_{w\sim p,\,c\sim\mathcal{U}[0,2\pi]}\,2\cos(wu+c)\cos(wv+c), which yields the unbiased Monte Carlo estimator

k^D​(u,v)=2D​∑d=1Dcos⁡(wd​u+cd)​cos⁡(wd​v+cd),wd∼p,cd∼𝒰⁡[0,2​π].\widehat{k}_{D}(u,v)\;=\;\tfrac{2}{D}\sum_{d=1}^{D}\cos(w_{d}u+c_{d})\,\cos(w_{d}v+c_{d}),\qquad w_{d}\sim p,\ \ c_{d}\sim\mathcal{U}[0,2\pi]. (1)

The corresponding feature matrices Φ⁡(a)∈ℝn×D\Phi(a)\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times D} and Φ⁡(b)∈ℝk×D\Phi(b)\in\mathbb{R}^{k\times D} are dense; the forward pass costs 𝒪⁡((n+k)​D)\mathcal{O}((n+k)D). For the Laplace kernel k⁡(u−v)=exp⁡(−|u−v|)k(u-v)=\exp(-|u-v|) in one dimension, pp is the standard Cauchy distribution p⁡(w)=π−1​(1+w2)−1p(w)=\pi^{-1}(1+w^{2})^{-1}, sampled in our implementation via the inverse-CDF transform wd=tan⁡(π⁡(Ud−12))w_{d}=\tan(\pi(U_{d}-\tfrac{1}{2})), Ud∼𝒰⁡[0,1]U_{d}\sim\mathcal{U}[0,1]. This is the only spectral baseline that applies to the irregular node sets that motivate LAPLEX.

Experimental protocol.

n=k=216n=k=2^{16}, B=1B=1, a,b∼𝒩⁡(0,1)a,b\sim\mathcal{N}(0,1) independently and irregularly. For each D∈{1,2,4,…,2048}D\in\{1,2,4,\ldots,2048\} we evaluate the RFF estimator 1010 times with independent random features (wd,cd)d=1D(w_{d},c_{d})_{d=1}^{D} and report the median and the [min,max][\min,\max] range of the relative ℓ2\ell_{2} error ‖y^−y‖2/‖y‖2\|\widehat{y}-y\|_{2}/\|y\|_{2}, with y=x⊤​K​(a,b)y=x^{\!\top}\!K(a,b) computed by LAPLEX (which we verified against an 𝒪⁡(n2)\mathcal{O}(n^{2}) dense matmul up to n=2048n=2048, relative error <10−6<10^{-6}). Gradients ∂L/∂a\partial L/\partial a and ∂L/∂b\partial L/\partial b are computed by back-propagating L=𝟏⊤​y^L=\mathbf{1}^{\!\top}\!\widehat{y} through either the RFF estimator or LAPLEX.

Value error.

The empirical value error tracks the classical 𝒪⁡(1/D)\mathcal{O}(1/\sqrt{D}) concentration rate (Fig. 6(b) of the main text): the median error decreases from ∼4.5\sim\!4.5 at D=1D=1 to ∼0.076\sim\!0.076 at D=2048D=2048, a factor of ∼59×\sim\!59\times for a 2048×2048\times increase in DD (2048≈45\sqrt{2048}\approx 45). The [min,max][\min,\max] band stays narrow because the summands in (1) are bounded by 11 and Hoeffding’s inequality applies; the worst-case-to-median ratio across seeds is at most ∼2×\sim\!2\times for every tested DD.

F.2 Gradient with respect to anchor positions

A theoretical obstruction.

Differentiating the RFF estimator with respect to the node locations introduces a frequency factor:

∂k^D​(u,v)∂u=−2D∑d=1Dwdsin(wdu+cd)cos(wdv+cd).\frac{\partial\widehat{k}_{D}(u,v)}{\partial u}\;=\;-\tfrac{2}{D}\sum_{d=1}^{D}w_{d}\,\sin(w_{d}u+c_{d})\,\cos(w_{d}v+c_{d}). (2)

Each summand in (2) is bounded only by |wd||w_{d}|, and for the Laplace kernel wdw_{d} is drawn from the standard Cauchy distribution, whose second moment is infinite. Two consequences follow.

(i) The estimator has unbounded variance, so the standard concentration tools (Hoeffding, Bernstein) do not bound its deviations. (ii) Sums of DD i.i.d. Cauchy variables are themselves Cauchy: by closure of the Cauchy family under convolution, no central limit theorem at the canonical 1/D1/\sqrt{D} rate holds. The error distribution is therefore heavy-tailed, dominated by occasional large-frequency draws, and concentration as D→∞D\to\infty is not guaranteed [27]. LAPLEX, in contrast, delivers gradients that are exact by construction (up to float32 round-off) at the same 𝒪⁡(n​log⁡n)\mathcal{O}(n\log n) cost as the forward pass.

Empirical verification.

Figure 18 reports the relative error of y^\widehat{y}, ∇aL^\widehat{\nabla_{a}L}, and ∇bL^\widehat{\nabla_{b}L} (medians and [min,max][\min,\max] ranges across 1010 seeds). Three qualitative differences from the value case are visible.

(i) Broken 1/D1/\sqrt{D} scaling. The gradient error with respect to aa decreases only by a factor of ∼26\sim\!26 between D=1D=1 and D=2048D=2048, against ∼57\sim\!57 for the value; the gradient with respect to bb does not measurably decrease at all, saturating around 200​–​460%200\text{--}460\% relative error across the entire sweep.

(ii) Heavy tails. The worst-case-to-median ratio across seeds exceeds 10×10\times for ∇aL^\widehat{\nabla_{a}L} at several values of DD and reaches over 100×100\times for ∇bL^\widehat{\nabla_{b}L}, a direct manifestation of the Cauchy-sampled frequency factor in (2).

(iii) Asymmetry between ∇a\nabla_{a} and ∇b\nabla_{b}. Because the loss L=𝟏⊤​(x⊤​K)L=\mathbf{1}^{\!\top}(x^{\!\top}\!K) sums the xx-weighted entries over rows, the two gradient norms differ by two orders of magnitude in our setup (‖∇a‖≈2.5⋅106\|\nabla_{a}\|\approx 2.5\cdot 10^{6} versus ‖∇b‖≈2.3⋅104\|\nabla_{b}\|\approx 2.3\cdot 10^{4}), so the same absolute Cauchy-driven noise produces dramatically larger relative error on ∇b\nabla_{b}. Whichever coordinate produces a smaller-norm gradient is where RFF fails first.

Takeaway.

RFF is a useful approximation when one needs a fixed-kernel value estimate and can choose a feature count large enough for the desired tolerance. It is a poor replacement for LAPLEX as a learnable operator over Laplace anchors. At the runtime crossover its value error is still large; at feature counts where the value becomes accurate it is much slower; and the anchor-gradient estimator has unbounded variance because the Laplace spectrum is Cauchy. LAPLEX computes the same kernel product exactly, including anchor gradients, at a cost independent of any feature dimension.

Appendix G Logistic regression: full 𝝉\boldsymbol{\tau}-sweep for the frozen baseline

The main text reports the frozen-projection experiment at a single representative inverse-temperature, τ=0.1\tau=0.1. Here we expose the temperature sweep; see Table 4. The point is not to tune aggressively, but to show that the behavior is stable: sharp kernels behave like learned gathering, smoother kernels behave more like random projections, and a wide middle range remains competitive. CountSketch, PCA, and RP are repeated from Table 1 for reference.

Observations.

The qualitative picture extends the main-text reading: (i) small τ\tau (0.010.01, 0.050.05) acts approximately like a sharp gather and tracks CountSketch closely, with a peak near m=250m=250 and a slow decay afterwards; (ii) intermediate τ\tau (0.10.1, 0.50.5) interpolates between sharp and smooth and is the most robust to changes in mm, peaking later and not collapsing; (iii) large τ\tau (1.01.0) behaves like a smoothed RP and plateaus around 30%30\%. At m=1000m=1000 the best frozen-LAPLEX configurations (τ∈{0.1,0.5}\tau\in\{0.1,0.5\}) are the only methods that maintain >31%>31\% accuracy across the full sweep – every non-LAPLEX baseline (CountSketch, PCA, RP) is below 30%30\% at that size. The choice τ=0.1\tau=0.1 used in the main text is a reasonable default; in practice τ\tau can simply be made trainable, in which case it converges to a value in this same range.

Appendix H Classification heads: full details

The structured-head experiment is intentionally simple: the backbone is kept fixed while only the final classification layer is replaced, allowing us to study which low-parameter head most faithfully reproduces the original classifier. The main text reports the headline comparison; here we include the training configuration, exact parameter counts, validation accuracies, and optimization curves.

As backbone models, we use Swin-T [20] and MaxViT-T [30], both with publicly available pretrained weights on ImageNet-1k.

Setup.

For Swin-T, the original head is a single linear layer W∈ℝc×fW\in\mathbb{R}^{c\times f}; for MaxViT-T, it is the linear component of a two-layer MLP with W1∈ℝf2×f1W_{1}\in\mathbb{R}^{f_{2}\times f_{1}} and W2∈ℝc×f2W_{2}\in\mathbb{R}^{c\times f_{2}}, where c=1000c=1000 denotes the ImageNet-1k classes. As baselines, we report both the original pretrained head and a randomly initialized full-rank dense head. We then compare two structured low-parameter alternatives at matched rank rr:

(i) the LAPLEX head,

LAPLEX(r)=∑i=1rwi​Li,Li∈ℝc×f,\mathrm{LAPLEX}^{(r)}\;=\;\sum_{i=1}^{r}w_{i}\,L_{i},\qquad L_{i}\in\mathbb{R}^{c\times f},

where each LiL_{i} is a LAPLEX matrix parameterized by an independent anchor pair (ai,bi)(a_{i},b_{i}) and wiw_{i} are trained scalar mixing weights;

(ii) the low-rank factorization,

LowRank(r)=U​V⊤,U∈ℝc×r,V∈ℝf×r.\mathrm{LowRank}^{(r)}=UV^{\!\top},\qquad U\in\mathbb{R}^{c\times r},\quad V\in\mathbb{R}^{f\times r}.

All structured heads are trained with the backbone frozen on the full ImageNet-1k training split. To ensure fair comparison, the optimization setup is kept identical across all ranks and both backbones (Table 5).

Results.

Table 6 reports parameter counts and achieved accuracy for both Swin-T and MaxViT-T. Across both backbones, the LAPLEX(r) head consistently outperforms LowRank(r) at matched parameter budgets, with the largest margin observed at low rank (r=4r=4). As the rank increases, performance improves for both methods; however, LAPLEX(r) remains superior across all settings. At r=16r=16, LAPLEX(r) reduces the gap to the original pretrained head to approximately 1%1\% on MaxViT-T and 4%4\% on Swin-T, while using only ∼\sim5% and ∼\sim4% of the original parameters, respectively.

Figure 19 further illustrates training dynamics. Across all ranks and both backbones, LAPLEX(r) exhibits faster convergence and consistently lower training and validation loss compared to LowRank(r), reaching equal or better final values.

Appendix I Density modeling with a Laplace-kernel covariance: full details

The density experiment is the most concrete demonstration of what the Gram primitive buys: a high-dimensional covariance model whose structure is learned from flat data, rather than imposed by image geometry. The point is to show how LAPLEX enables efficient and exact computation of the weighted Gramian A⊤​diag​(D)​AA^{\!\top}\!\mathrm{diag}(D)A on high-dimensional data, the central primitive that unlocks second-order methods (Gauss–Newton, natural gradient, Fisher-based curvature, Woodbury-accelerated Gaussian likelihoods) at scales where forming the corresponding n×nn\!\times\!n covariance is infeasible. We use Gaussian density modeling as the running illustration: a Gaussian density on flattened images is fully specified by the mean and a structured covariance, and the quality of that covariance is directly visible through samples and MAP reconstructions. The same primitive underlies every other second-order application of LAPLEX in this paper.

All models operate on the flattened pixel vector.

Throughout this section, every model – LAPLEX, the dense low-rank baseline, the empirical-covariance truncation, and the unconstrained empirical Gaussian reference – treats each image as a flat nn-dimensional vector with no spatial bias built in: pixels are not arranged on a grid, no convolution or patching is applied, and no positional encoding is provided. Whatever spatial-color structure the learned covariance recovers must therefore be discovered end-to-end from the data itself.

Why ImageNette-320.

We benchmark on flattened ImageNette-320320 (n=3202⋅3=307,200n{=}320^{2}\!\cdot\!3{=}307{,}200, N=9,469N{=}9{,}469 training images, 1010 classes). The pixel dimension is large enough that natural images display rich spatial-color structure and the unconstrained empirical covariance Σ^∈ℝn×n\hat{\Sigma}\!\in\!\mathbb{R}^{n\times n} is no longer storable in practice (∼354\sim\!354 GB in fp32). At the same time, the modest number of training images (N≪nN{\ll}n) lets us still evaluate the full empirical Gaussian exactly through an N×NN\!\times\!N “SVD trick”: the top eigenvectors of Σ^\hat{\Sigma} are recovered from the centered-data Gram Xc​Xc⊤/(N−1)X_{c}X_{c}^{\!\top}/(N{-}1) without ever materializing the n×nn\!\times\!n matrix. This combination makes ImageNette-320320 a regime where structured-covariance parameterizations such as LAPLEX face a non-trivial empirical-covariance ceiling, and where matched-budget dense families are severely crippled by their effective-rank constraint.

Low-rank Gaussian modeling in high dimensions.

A standard recipe for building a multivariate Gaussian density 𝒩⁡(m,Σ)\mathcal{N}(m,\Sigma) in high-dimensional ℝn\mathbb{R}^{n} when the full n×nn\!\times\!n covariance is neither storable nor factorisable is to lift a lower kk-dimensional latent Gaussian33 3 We parameterise Σk\Sigma_{k} through its Cholesky factor. 𝒩⁡(0,Σk)\mathcal{N}(0,\Sigma_{k}) through a linear map and add diagonal noise:

x=m+F​z+d⊙ε,z∼𝒩⁡(0,Σk),ε∼𝒩⁡(0,In),x\;=\;m\;+\;F\,z\;+\;d\odot\varepsilon,\quad z\sim\mathcal{N}(0,\Sigma_{k}),\;\varepsilon\sim\mathcal{N}(0,I_{n}), (3)

which induces

Σ=D+F​Σk​F⊤=D+W​W⊤,D=diag⁡(d2),W=F​L,\Sigma\;=\;D+F\,\Sigma_{k}\,F^{\!\top}\;=\;D+WW^{\!\top},\qquad D=\mathrm{diag}(d^{2}),\quad W=F\,L,

where LL is the Cholesky factor of Σk=L​L⊤\Sigma_{k}=LL^{\!\top}. This diagonal-plus-low-rank factor-analysis template underlies probabilistic PCA [29], mixtures of PPCA and factor analyzers [28, 12], EPLL-style patch-based image priors [35], and efficient GMMs of natural images [25].

The key practical reason for the template is the Woodbury identity, which reduces log-likelihood evaluation from operations of size n×nn\!\times\!n to matrix–vector operations of size n×kn\!\times\!k and a determinant of size k×kk\!\times\!k:

Σ−1\displaystyle\Sigma^{-1} =D−1−D−1​W​(Ik+W⊤​D−1​W)−1​W⊤​D−1,\displaystyle=D^{-1}-D^{-1}W\bigl(I_{k}+W^{\!\top}D^{-1}W\bigr)^{-1}W^{\!\top}D^{-1}, (4)
logdetΣ\displaystyle\log\det\Sigma =logdetD+logdet(Ik+W⊤D−1W).\displaystyle=\log\det D+\log\det\bigl(I_{k}+W^{\!\top}D^{-1}W\bigr). (5)

The bottleneck is therefore the k×kk\!\times\!k capacitance matrix M=Ik+W⊤​D−1​WM=I_{k}+W^{\!\top}D^{-1}W.

The key design choice is the parameterization of FF. We compare two matched-budget regimes on the same template (3): a small budget (∼2.2\sim\!2.2M trainable parameters) at which we run the simplest LAPLEX instantiation alongside two dense baselines, and a larger budget (∼3.5\sim\!3.5M) at which we contrast the natural multi-component extension of LAPLEX against the same two dense baselines re-trained at the larger rank. Across both budgets we evaluate four kinds of FF:

  • •

    LAPLEX (single-component, I=1I{=}1): F=diag⁡(w)​A​L⊤F{=}\mathrm{diag}(w)\,A\,L^{\!\top}, where A∈ℝn×klaplexA\!\in\!\mathbb{R}^{n\times k_{\mathrm{laplex}}} is the phased Laplace kernel with continuous anchor parameters and L∈ℝklaplex×klaplexL\!\in\!\mathbb{R}^{k_{\mathrm{laplex}}\times k_{\mathrm{laplex}}} is lower-triangular with positive diagonal;

  • •

    LAPLEX (multi-component, I=2I{=}2): F=∑i=1Idiag⁡(wi)​A​Li⊤F{=}\sum_{i=1}^{I}\mathrm{diag}(w_{i})\,A\,L_{i}^{\!\top} with AA shared and per-component weights wiw_{i} and arbitrary factors Li∈ℝklaplex×klaplexL_{i}\!\in\!\mathbb{R}^{k_{\mathrm{laplex}}\times k_{\mathrm{laplex}}} (no triangular constraint);

  • •

    dense low-rank baseline: fully free F∈ℝn×klow-rankF\!\in\!\mathbb{R}^{n\times k_{\text{low-rank}}};

  • •

    empirical-covariance truncation (probabilistic PCA): the top kcovk_{\mathrm{cov}} eigenvectors of Σ^\hat{\Sigma}, with Σ=Vkcov​Λ​Vkcov⊤+σ2​(I−Vkcov​Vkcov⊤)\Sigma{=}V_{k_{\mathrm{cov}}}\Lambda V_{k_{\mathrm{cov}}}^{\!\top}+\sigma^{2}(I{-}V_{k_{\mathrm{cov}}}V_{k_{\mathrm{cov}}}^{\!\top}) and σ2\sigma^{2} from [29];

  • •

    (reference, not matched-budget) the full empirical Gaussian 𝒩⁡(m^,Σ^+ε​I)\mathcal{N}(\hat{m},\hat{\Sigma}+\varepsilon I) with optimal ridge ε\varepsilon, evaluated exactly via the SVD trick.

The matched ranks for each budget regime are determined algebraically by the budget formulas Plaplex(I)=n⁡(1+I)+I​klaplex 2+𝒪⁡(klaplex)P_{\mathrm{laplex}}^{(I)}{=}n(1{+}I)+I\,k_{\mathrm{laplex}}^{\,2}+\mathcal{O}(k_{\mathrm{laplex}}), Plow​-​rank=n+n​klow-rank+𝒪⁡(klow-rank2)P_{\mathrm{low\text{-}rank}}{=}n+n\,k_{\text{low-rank}}+\mathcal{O}(k_{\text{low-rank}}^{2}), Pcov=n+n​kcov+kcovP_{\mathrm{cov}}{=}n+n\,k_{\mathrm{cov}}+k_{\mathrm{cov}}. At ∼2.2\sim\!2.2M they pin klaplex=1000k_{\mathrm{laplex}}{=}1000 (I=1I{=}1), klow-rank=6k_{\text{low-rank}}{=}6 and kcov=6k_{\mathrm{cov}}{=}6. At ∼3.5\sim\!3.5M (matched to multi LAPLEX, which has exactly 3,538,0013{,}538{,}001 trainables) the dense families lift to klow-rank=11k_{\text{low-rank}}{=}11 and kcov=11k_{\mathrm{cov}}{=}11, an effective rank still nearly two orders of magnitude below the klaplex=1000k_{\mathrm{laplex}}{=}1000 that LAPLEX sustains in either regime.

Sampling and MAP reconstruction.

From the generative form (3) both sampling and reconstruction are natural. Sampling draws z∼𝒩⁡(0,Ik)z\sim\mathcal{N}(0,I_{k}) and ε∼𝒩⁡(0,In)\varepsilon\sim\mathcal{N}(0,I_{n}) and returns x=m+W​z+d⊙εx{=}m+Wz+d\odot\varepsilon; for the PCA reference (no noise term, latent z∼𝒩⁡(0,Λ)z\sim\mathcal{N}(0,\Lambda) with Λ=diag⁡(λ1,…,λkcov)\Lambda{=}\mathrm{diag}(\lambda_{1},\ldots,\lambda_{k_{\mathrm{cov}}}) the top-kcovk_{\mathrm{cov}} eigenvalues) this reduces to x=m^+Vkcov​Λ1/2​zx{=}\hat{m}+V_{k_{\mathrm{cov}}}\Lambda^{1/2}z. MAP reconstruction of an observed image xx under the generative model is, for our kernel and dense-LR variants, a Woodbury-accelerated posterior mean: the MAP latent z∗=arg⁡maxz⁡p⁡(z∣x)z^{\!*}=\arg\max_{z}p(z\mid x) is the unique solution of

(Ik+F⊤​D−1​F)​z∗=F⊤​D−1​(x−m),x^MAP=m+F​z∗,(I_{k}+F^{\!\top}D^{-1}F)\,z^{\!*}\;=\;F^{\!\top}D^{-1}(x-m),\qquad\hat{x}_{\mathrm{MAP}}\;=\;m+F\,z^{\!*}, (6)

obtained by one k×kk\!\times\!k Cholesky solve. For the empirical-covariance truncation the noise term vanishes and the MAP coincides with the orthogonal projection x^MAP=m^+Vkcov​Vkcov⊤​(x−m^)\hat{x}_{\mathrm{MAP}}=\hat{m}+V_{k_{\mathrm{cov}}}V_{k_{\mathrm{cov}}}^{\!\top}(x-\hat{m}).

Training and evaluation.

We train all variants of LAPLEX and the dense low-rank baseline on flattened ImageNette-320320 for 2525 epochs with Adam (lr 2×10−32{\times}10^{-3}, batch 6464); the Gram matrices Gi​jG_{ij} and the Cholesky of the capacitance MM run in fp64 via a custom decoupled-lookback scan, the rest in fp32. The empirical-covariance truncation is computed in closed form via the SVD trick – no training – and the same eigendecomposition serves both budget regimes (kcov=6k_{\mathrm{cov}}{=}6 and kcov=11k_{\mathrm{cov}}{=}11 are just two truncation depths of the same spectrum). At the ∼2.2\sim\!2.2M-parameter budget the three matched models have 2,231,8012{,}231{,}801 (LAPLEX I=1I{=}1), 2,150,4422{,}150{,}442 (dense klow-rank=6k_{\text{low-rank}}{=}6) and 2,150,4062{,}150{,}406 (PCA kcov=6k_{\mathrm{cov}}{=}6) trainables (matched within 4%4\%). At the ∼3.5\sim\!3.5M-parameter budget they have 3,538,0013{,}538{,}001 (LAPLEX I=2I{=}2, two arbitrary LiL_{i}), 3,686,4663{,}686{,}466 (dense klow-rank=11k_{\text{low-rank}}{=}11) and 3,686,4013{,}686{,}401 (PCA kcov=11k_{\mathrm{cov}}{=}11) trainables (matched within 5%5\%). The unconstrained ridge-regularized empirical Gaussian ceiling sits above both: with optimal ε=10−2\varepsilon{=}10^{-2} (selected by val LL) it effectively requires ∼2.9\sim\!2.9 B parameters to store the centered training data XcX_{c} and the recovered spectrum – roughly 1,300×1{,}300{\times} more than the small matched set and ∼820×\sim\!820{\times} more than the larger matched set.

Construction of the multi-component variant.

At the ∼2.2\sim\!2.2M-parameter budget LAPLEX reduces to a single F=diag⁡(w)​A​L⊤F{=}\mathrm{diag}(w)\,A\,L^{\!\top} with shared phased Laplace kernel AA and one lower-triangular factor L∈ℝklaplex×klaplexL\!\in\!\mathbb{R}^{k_{\mathrm{laplex}}\times k_{\mathrm{laplex}}}. At the larger ∼3.5\sim\!3.5M-parameter budget we evaluate the natural multi-component enrichment in which we allow a sum of II structured factors, sharing AA but with per-component weights and per-component LiL_{i}:

F=∑i=1Idiag⁡(wi)​A​Li⊤,Li∈ℝklaplex×klaplex​(arbitrary, no triangular constraint),F\;=\;\sum_{i=1}^{I}\mathrm{diag}(w_{i})\,A\,L_{i}^{\!\top},\quad L_{i}\!\in\!\mathbb{R}^{k_{\mathrm{laplex}}\times k_{\mathrm{laplex}}}\ \text{(arbitrary, no triangular constraint)}, (7)

which yields Σ=D+F​F⊤=D+∑i,jdiag⁡(wi)​A​Li⊤​Lj​A⊤​diag​(wj)\Sigma=D+FF^{\!\top}=D+\sum_{i,j}\mathrm{diag}(w_{i})\,AL_{i}^{\!\top}L_{j}\,A^{\!\top}\mathrm{diag}(w_{j}). The klaplex×klaplexk_{\mathrm{laplex}}\!\times\!k_{\mathrm{laplex}} capacitance matrix factorizes as

M=Iklaplex+F⊤​D−1​F=Iklaplex+∑i,j=1ILi​Gi​j​Lj⊤,Gi​j=A⊤​diag​(wi​wj/d2)​A.M=I_{k_{\mathrm{laplex}}}+F^{\!\top}D^{-1}F\;=\;I_{k_{\mathrm{laplex}}}+\sum_{i,j=1}^{I}L_{i}\,G_{ij}\,L_{j}^{\!\top},\quad G_{ij}=A^{\!\top}\mathrm{diag}(w_{i}w_{j}/d^{2})\,A.

By symmetry Gi​j=Gj​iG_{ij}{=}G_{ji} there are only I⁡(I+1)/2I(I{+}1)/2 distinct Grams – each computed by the three-real-Gram identity in 𝒪⁡(n2+n​klaplex)\mathcal{O}(n^{2}+n\,k_{\mathrm{laplex}}), so the total Gramian cost is 𝒪⁡(I⁡(I+1)/2⋅n2)\mathcal{O}\!\bigl(I(I{+}1)/2\cdot n^{2}\bigr), while the Cholesky of MM remains 𝒪⁡(klaplex3)\mathcal{O}(k_{\mathrm{laplex}}^{3}). The rank of Σ−D\Sigma{-}D is unchanged at klaplexk_{\mathrm{laplex}} (since F∈ℝn×klaplexF\!\in\!\mathbb{R}^{n\times k_{\mathrm{laplex}}} in spite of the sum), but the family of representable FF is strictly richer than the single-component case: arbitrary LiL_{i} break the lower-triangular restriction and the sum cannot in general be realised by a single (w,L)(w,L) pair. The parameterization carries an 𝒪⁡(klaplex)\mathcal{O}(k_{\mathrm{laplex}}) gauge symmetry Li↦Li​QL_{i}\!\mapsto\!L_{i}Q for any Q∈O⁡(klaplex)Q\!\in\!O(k_{\mathrm{laplex}}) applied uniformly; this leaves F​F⊤FF^{\!\top} invariant but does not obstruct Adam empirically. We instantiate the construction at I∈{2,3}I{\in}\{2,3\}, both with full klaplex×klaplexk_{\mathrm{laplex}}\!\times\!k_{\mathrm{laplex}} LiL_{i}.

Results.

The picture (Fig. 20, Tab. 7) is qualitatively unambiguous at both budget regimes. At ∼2.2\sim\!2.2M trainables (Tab. 7, rows 1, 3, 4) both budget-matched dense families collapse to ∼6\sim\!6-dimensional latents–an unavoidable consequence of the linear cost of storing VkcovV_{k_{\mathrm{cov}}} or the dense FF, which pins kcov≈klow-rank≈6k_{\mathrm{cov}}\!\approx\!k_{\text{low-rank}}\!\approx\!6 at n=307,200n{=}307{,}200. Neither family can encode any spatial smoothness, and they produce qualitatively unstructured samples (Tab. 7, rows 3–4; not shown in Fig. 20). LAPLEX converts the same budget into an effective rank of klaplex=1000k_{\mathrm{laplex}}{=}1000 and yields spatially coherent color blobs (Fig. 20, middle)–contiguous patches of green, brown or blue–precisely because the optimized Laplace anchors α,γ\alpha,\gamma embed nearby pixels close in kernel distance, even though the input is a flat 307,200307{,}200-vector and the model is strictly linear in its latent representation. On test log-likelihood, LAPLEX (I=1I{=}1) gains ≈+154,000\approx\!+154{,}000 nats over the PCA truncation (198,549198{,}549 vs. 44,81144{,}811) and ≈+160,000\approx\!+160{,}000 over the dense low-rank baseline (198,549198{,}549 vs. 38,39538{,}395); on per-church MAP RMSE it reaches 0.1290.129, well ahead of 0.2270.227 (PCA) and 0.2300.230 (dense).

At the larger ∼3.5\sim\!3.5M-parameter budget (Fig. 20, centre-right, and Tab. 7, row 2 alongside the correspondingly-rescaled dense rows) the multi-component extension F=diag⁡(w1)​A​L1⊤+diag⁡(w2)​A​L2⊤F{=}\mathrm{diag}(w_{1})AL_{1}^{\!\top}+\mathrm{diag}(w_{2})AL_{2}^{\!\top} with arbitrary LiL_{i} lifts LAPLEX to test LL 229,607229{,}607 and church RMSE 0.1150.115 (+31,058+31{,}058 nats and −11%-11\% RMSE relative to I=1I{=}1). The same ∼3.5\sim\!3.5M budget allotted to the dense families merely lifts their effective rank from ∼6\sim\!6 to ∼11\sim\!11, two orders of magnitude below klaplex=1000k_{\mathrm{laplex}}{=}1000, and their samples remain qualitatively unstructured (LL 66,10766{,}107 and 67,83467{,}834 for dense klow-rank=11k_{\text{low-rank}}{=}11 and PPCA kcov=11k_{\mathrm{cov}}{=}11 respectively, vs. 229,607229{,}607 for LAPLEX I=2I{=}2 at the same budget). Pushing the construction one component further to I=3I{=}3 (∼4.84\sim\!4.84M trainables, Tab. 7, row 3 and Fig. 20, right) yields test LL 238,578238{,}578 and church RMSE 0.1140.114, a marginal +8,971+8{,}971-nat / −0.001-0.001-RMSE improvement on top of I=2I{=}2 at +37%+37\% extra trainables – substantially less per-parameter than the I=1→I=2I{=}1{\to}I{=}2 jump and a clear sign that the multi-component arithmetic is approaching the empirical-Gaussian ceiling. The optimized single-τ\tau kernel scale itself shifts from τ=0.029\tau{=}0.029 (I=1I{=}1) to τ=0.052\tau{=}0.052 (I=2I{=}2), suggesting the two components specialize to different correlation length-scales rather than converging to redundant copies. Across-image generalization mirrors the church result: on ten held-out images, one uniformly-random per ImageNette class (Fig. 21), mean MAP RMSE drops monotonically with II: 0.1190.119 (I=1I{=}1), 0.1050.105 (I=2I{=}2, −12%-12\% vs. I=1I{=}1), 0.1020.102 (I=3I{=}3, −14%-14\% vs. I=1I{=}1, −3%-3\% on top of I=2I{=}2), at +59%+59\% and +117%+117\% trainable parameters respectively. Every one of the ten I=2I{=}2 reconstructions has strictly lower RMSE than its I=1I{=}1 counterpart (per-class gain −8%-8\% for gas pump up to −20%-20\% for parachute); the I=3I{=}3 row matches or beats I=2I{=}2 on every class at the 10−310^{-3} level (strictly improving in 88 of 1010, exactly tied on French horn at 0.1290.129, and within 10−410^{-4} on golf ball at 0.0670.067), but the per-class improvements are visibly smaller, again consistent with the diminishing-returns trend in test LL.

Comparison to the unconstrained ceiling.

For reference we also evaluate the ridge-regularized empirical Gaussian 𝒩⁡(m^,Σ^+ε​I)\mathcal{N}(\hat{m},\hat{\Sigma}+\varepsilon I), computed exactly via the SVD trick. The optimal ε=10−2\varepsilon{=}10^{-2} (selected by val LL) yields test LL 315,549315{,}549 and per-image MAP RMSE 0.0750.075, at the cost of ∼2.9\sim\!2.9 B effective parameters (N⋅n+nN{\cdot}n+n: the storage of all centered training images plus the mean) or, equivalently, the entire empirical covariance (∼47\sim\!47 B unique entries). LAPLEX climbs the ceiling monotonically with II: ≈63%\approx\!63\% at I=1I{=}1 (∼1,300×\sim\!1{,}300{\times} fewer parameters than Σ^\hat{\Sigma}), ≈73%\approx\!73\% at I=2I{=}2 (∼820×\sim\!820{\times} fewer), and ≈76%\approx\!76\% at I=3I{=}3 (∼600×\sim\!600{\times} fewer), with samples (Fig. 20, left vs. centre-left, centre-right, and right) that are visually only marginally less detailed than the ceiling, while the matched-budget dense families do not approach either at either of the two budgets we evaluated. The marginal closure shrinks as II grows (+10+10 percentage points I=1→I=2I{=}1{\to}I{=}2 vs. only +3+3 points I=2→I=3I{=}2{\to}I{=}3), suggesting that the kernel-structured parameterization is effectively compressing the empirical second-order statistics rather than discovering them de novo: the first one or two components already absorb most of the spatially-coherent variance and additional components are forced to fit progressively higher-frequency residuals.

Takeaway.

The most striking finding of this experiment is qualitative and visible by eye in Fig. 20: LAPLEX at klaplex=1000k_{\mathrm{laplex}}{=}1000, trained on flat 307,200307{,}200-vectors with no positional encoding, has learned that pixel colors are correlated by spatial position. Already at the small ∼2.2\sim\!2.2M-parameter budget the I=1I{=}1 sample (Fig. 20, middle) shows contiguous patches of green, brown or blue – the kind of soft color blobs found in natural-image priors – and its MAP reconstruction (Fig. 21, middle row) preserves the church silhouette and sky–ground gradient, whereas both budget-matched dense families collapse to spatially uniform noise. The only spatial information available to the model is what gets baked into the optimized continuous Laplace anchors (α,γ)(\alpha,\gamma), so the learned index-level parameters have embedded the planar pixel grid into the covariance structure. The multi-component extension (Fig. 20, centre-right and right) inherits the same qualitative behaviour at all II tested, and lifts test LL monotonically with II: +31,058+31{,}058 nats I=1→I=2I{=}1{\to}I{=}2 (at +59%+59\% trainables) and +8,971+8{,}971 nats I=2→I=3I{=}2{\to}I{=}3 (at +37%+37\% extra trainables on top of I=2I{=}2), each step requiring no architectural change beyond Eq. (7). The marginal I=3I{=}3 gain is already much smaller than the I=2I{=}2 jump – a clean diminishing-returns curve toward the empirical-Gaussian ceiling. The dense families re-trained at ∼3.5\sim\!3.5M parameters still cannot escape their effective rank of ∼11\sim\!11. Within the Gaussian families tested here – at either matched budget – LAPLEX is the only parameterization that turns a few million Woodbury parameters into coherent ImageNette-320320 samples and reconstructions; dense low-rank (klow-rank∈{6,11}k_{\text{low-rank}}{\in}\{6,11\}) and empirical-covariance truncation (kcov∈{6,11}k_{\mathrm{cov}}{\in}\{6,11\}) remain too rank-limited to do so.
